questions.stem: A retailer's support agent runs on the Claude Agent SDK and can issue refunds through an MCP tool, mcp__billing__issue_refund. To keep conversations fast, an engineer added every billing tool by bare name to allowedTools. Company policy requires a human supervisor to approve any refund above $500, so the team also wrote a canUseTool callback that allows small refunds immediately and parks larger ones in a supervisor queue until someone approves. The query options do not set permissionMode. During staging tests, a $1,200 refund executed with no supervisor involvement, and the callback's logs show it was never invoked for that call. What change most directly enforces the approval policy?

options.text: Set permissionMode to "dontAsk" so the SDK stops auto-approving and routes every refund call, including tools listed in allowedTools, to canUseTool for a decision.
options.rationale: Wrong. dontAsk never calls canUseTool and does not revoke allow rules: it denies anything that would prompt, and tools pre-approved by allowedTools still run, so the $1,200 refund would still execute.

options.text: Remove the refund tool from allowedTools and set permissionMode to "default" explicitly, so refund calls reach canUseTool, which allows small refunds and queues large ones for a supervisor.
options.rationale: Correct. A bare allowedTools entry auto-approves every call to that tool, and auto-approved calls never reach canUseTool; removing it lets refunds reach the callback, and setting default explicitly avoids starting in auto mode, where a classifier decides instead.

options.text: Keep allowedTools unchanged and add a system prompt rule, repeated in the refund tool's description, telling the agent to call a request_supervisor tool and wait for approval before any refund over $500.
options.rationale: Wrong. A prompt rule, even one repeated in the tool description, only steers Claude and is not enforced by the SDK; the bare allow rule still auto-approves the refund whenever Claude skips the step or does not wait.

options.text: Move refunds into a dedicated billing subagent whose AgentDefinition lists only the refund tool in its tools field.
options.rationale: Wrong. The tools field controls which tools the subagent has, not whether calls are approved, and the subagent inherits the parent's permission rules, so the bare allow rule still auto-approves the refund.

questions.explanation: Agent SDK permission checks run in a fixed order: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, then canUseTool. A call approved at an earlier step never reaches the callback, so a human approval gate has to sit on a path the call actually reaches (no bare allow rule for that tool, or a PreToolUse hook, which runs before every other step).
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the SDK permissions and user-input pages say a bare allowedTools entry auto-approves every call to that tool and auto-approved calls never reach canUseTool; the best-practices page says Manual (default) mode asks before MCP tools, so an unlisted refund call falls through to the callback. Drift: before TypeScript Agent SDK v0.3.286 (2026-09-30), omitting permissionMode was the same as passing default, so exam-era material will not mention auto mode; the key is unchanged because setting default explicitly is harmless there. Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractors a and c lengthened with still-wrong detail (dontAsk framed as routing allowedTools calls to canUseTool; the prompt rule also placed in the tool description) and their rationales updated; key reworded from "fall through to" to "reach" with no tested fact removed.

questions.stem: A market-intelligence product uses a research agent built on the Claude Agent SDK. One agent handles every query sequentially. Narrow questions such as "When was Vendor X founded?" work well, but broad requests such as "Compare pricing, security certifications, and integrations for the eight leading vendors" fill the context window, trigger compaction, and lose early findings. The team adds a lead agent that delegates to research subagents. In the first test of the broad request, three subagents researched the same two vendors and no subagent covered vendors six through eight. Simple lookups now also spawn several subagents and cost far more than before. Which change best fixes both problems?

options.text: Return each subagent's full transcript, including every search result and intermediate note, to the lead agent so it can detect overlap and reassign uncovered vendors to idle subagents on its next turn.
options.rationale: Wrong. Only a subagent's final message is meant to return to the parent; piping full transcripts back rebuilds the context bloat the split was meant to remove and does nothing about cost on simple queries.

options.text: Replace delegation with a fixed prompt chain (search, then extract, then compare) that runs the same steps for every query, so work is never duplicated.
options.rationale: Wrong. Prompt chaining fits tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks; here the subtasks depend on the question (which vendors, which dimensions), which is where orchestrator-workers fits, and a fixed chain would still run every step on simple lookups.

options.text: Have the lead agent give each subagent a distinct objective (such as its assigned vendors), an output format, tool and source guidance, and clear boundaries, and scale subagent count to query complexity, answering simple lookups itself.
options.rationale: Correct. Anthropic's research system found that vague delegation makes subagents duplicate work and leave gaps, and that effort should scale with the query: a simple fact lookup needs one agent and a few tool calls, while complex research justifies many subagents.

options.text: Spawn a fixed set of subagents, one per vendor and dimension, for every query, each with a strict output template and tool list, so coverage is guaranteed regardless of how the question is phrased and simple lookups follow the same reliable path.
options.rationale: Wrong. This may fix coverage, but running the same full fan-out for every query makes simple lookups even more expensive; multi-agent runs use roughly 15x the tokens of a chat, so subagent count should track query complexity.

questions.explanation: Duplicated work and coverage gaps in orchestrator-worker systems usually trace back to vague delegation. The lead agent should hand each worker an objective, an output format, tool and source guidance, and boundaries, and should scale the number of workers to the query, because multi-agent runs cost many times more tokens than a single agent.
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractors a and d lengthened with still-wrong detail (intermediate notes in returned transcripts; per-subagent templates on a fixed fan-out) and d's rationale updated; key tightened with all four delegation elements and complexity scaling kept.

questions.stem: Your platform team maintains an internal developer assistant that calls the Messages API directly in a hand-written loop instead of using an SDK tool runner. The assistant enables the web_search server tool alongside two client tools that query internal build logs and the deploy calendar. Engineers report three symptoms: long research questions sometimes stop partway with no final answer, some requests return a truncated tool call that the loop then fails to execute, and the occasional request comes back as an empty end_turn response. You are rewriting the stop_reason handling. Which TWO behaviors should the new loop implement? Select TWO.

options.text: When stop_reason is "pause_turn", send the response's content back as the assistant turn, with the same tools, and call the API again so Claude can finish the server-side search work.
options.rationale: Correct. pause_turn means the server-side sampling loop for server tools such as web search hit its iteration limit; the documented handling is to send the assistant content back so Claude can continue.

options.text: When stop_reason is "tool_use", return the client tool_result blocks followed by a short text block such as "Here are the results" so Claude knows the user turn is complete.
options.rationale: Wrong. Text after tool_result blocks ends the assistant turn and teaches Claude to expect user text, a known cause of empty responses; when an unfinished web_search call is in the same response, the request fails with a 400.

options.text: When stop_reason is "end_turn" but content is empty, resend the identical messages array until Claude produces text.
options.rationale: Wrong. Claude already decided the turn is done, so resending it unchanged does not help; fix the message structure first and, as a last resort, add a continuation prompt in a new user message.

options.text: When stop_reason is "max_tokens" and the last content block is an incomplete tool_use, retry the request with a higher max_tokens instead of executing the partial tool call.
options.rationale: Correct. A tool_use block cut off by max_tokens is incomplete, and the documented fix is to resend the request with a larger max_tokens to get the full tool call.

options.text: When stop_reason is "refusal", treat it like an HTTP 5xx and let the client's automatic retry resend the same request to the same model.
options.rationale: Wrong. A refusal arrives as a normal HTTP 200 response, not an error, so transport retries never fire; the documented handling is to read stop_details and retry on a fallback model.

questions.explanation: Each stop_reason needs its own branch in a hand-written loop. pause_turn is continued by sending the assistant content back, and max_tokens with a truncated tool_use is retried with more tokens. Tool results go back on their own in the user message, empty end_turn responses need a structural fix or a new continuation prompt, and refusal is a 200 response handled with a fallback model.

questions.stem: An Agent SDK job sets max_turns=30. A run ends with a ResultMessage whose subtype is error_max_turns. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The result field holds the agent's last text output, flagged as partial so the caller can display it before deciding whether to rerun.
options.rationale: Wrong. The result field is present only on the success subtype; partial marking applies to a subagent's output in the Agent tool result, not to the top-level ResultMessage.

options.text: The session is discarded when the limit is hit, so the job must rerun the prompt from scratch with a higher max_turns.
options.rationale: Wrong. Error results still carry session_id, and the documented pattern is to resume the session with a higher limit rather than restart.

options.text: stop_reason is null, because the SDK ended the loop rather than the model, so no assistant stop value is carried over.
options.rationale: Wrong. On error results the loop produced, stop_reason carries the value from the last assistant response; null appears only on the result synthesized after a session crash.

options.text: total_cost_usd, num_turns, and session_id are still present, so you can log cost and resume the session with a higher limit.
options.rationale: Correct. Every result subtype carries cost, usage, num_turns, and session_id, so a turn-limited run can be logged and resumed.

questions.explanation: Check ResultMessage.subtype before reading result, because only success carries the result text. Every subtype still carries cost, usage, num_turns, and session_id, so a run that hits max_turns or max_budget_usd can be logged and resumed instead of restarted. A single-shot query() also raises after yielding the error result, so wrap the loop in a try block.
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractors a, b and c lengthened with wording their existing rationales already refute; key reworded ("record" to "log") with no tested fact removed.

questions.stem: Your main Agent SDK agent read a long error log, then delegates the fix to a custom subagent (not a fork). How does the subagent get the error details it needs?

options.text: The parent includes the relevant error lines and file paths in the prompt string it passes through the Agent tool.
options.rationale: Correct. A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context, and the Agent tool's prompt string is the only content passed from parent to subagent.

options.text: Nothing extra is needed: the subagent inherits the parent's conversation history and tool results.
options.rationale: Wrong. Only a fork inherits the parent conversation; a regular subagent does not receive the parent's history or tool results.

options.text: Set the subagent's model to "inherit" so it reuses the parent's context window.
options.rationale: Wrong. The "inherit" model value only makes the subagent use the main session's model; it shares no conversation context.

options.text: Append the log to the parent's system prompt, which subagents receive at startup.
options.rationale: Wrong. A subagent gets its own system prompt from its AgentDefinition, not the parent's system prompt.

questions.explanation: Context isolation works in both directions: a subagent's tool calls stay out of the parent's context, and the parent's history stays out of the subagent's. Whatever the subagent needs (file paths, error messages, decisions) must be written into the Agent tool's prompt.

questions.stem: A telecom's support assistant calls the Messages API in a hand-written loop. It enables the web_fetch server tool for reading public help-center articles and one client tool, get_account_status, which queries the billing system. Some responses come back with stop_reason "tool_use" and three content blocks: a short text block, a server_tool_use block for web_fetch with no matching result block, and a tool_use block for get_account_status. The loop assumes the fetch failed: it runs get_account_status, then sends a user message holding that tool_result followed by a text block saying "The article could not be loaded, answer without it." Every one of those follow-up requests fails with a 400 error, and customers get a generic apology. How should the loop continue these responses?

options.text: Treat the response like pause_turn: send the assistant content back unchanged with no new user message, let the API finish the fetch, and run get_account_status on the next response.
options.rationale: Wrong. A response that leaves a client tool_use waiting on you never has stop_reason pause_turn; you continue it by sending the client tool_result blocks, and every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result.

options.text: Add a tool_result for the server_tool_use id as well, with empty content and is_error set, so every tool call in the turn has a matching result before Claude continues.
options.rationale: Wrong. You do not answer server tools with tool_result blocks: the API runs them itself, and an unmatched server_tool_use in this response means the call is deferred, not failed.

options.text: Set disable_parallel_tool_use to true in tool_choice so Claude never groups web_fetch with a client tool, then resend the original request to get a fresh response.
options.rationale: Wrong. This works around a normal, documented state instead of handling it, pays for a new generation, and caps every response at one tool call, which slows ordinary multi-tool turns.

options.text: Send a user message that contains only the get_account_status tool_result, with the same tools array; the API then runs the deferred web_fetch and Claude continues its turn.
options.rationale: Correct. When Claude groups a server tool with a client tool, the API returns before running the server tool so you can run yours first; a reply of only tool_result blocks with the same tools lets the API run the fetch and continue.

questions.explanation: A tool_use response that holds a server_tool_use block with no matching result block means the server call was deferred so your client tools could run first, not that it failed. Reply with a user message of only tool_result blocks for your client tools and keep the same tools array; text after the results ends the turn early, and with an unresolved server tool the request fails with a 400.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the server-tools, handle-tool-calls and handling-stop-reasons pages: when a server tool and a client tool are called in the same parallel group, the API returns with stop_reason tool_use, the server_tool_use block has no result block and there is no other marker; reply with only the client tool_result blocks and the same tools array, the API runs the server tool on that request, and text after the results ends the turn early and fails with a 400 naming the unresolved server tool. Drift: exam-era material may describe server tools only through pause_turn and may not cover this deferred mixed-turn state, which current docs describe in detail.

questions.stem: Your team's code-generation service runs on the Claude Agent SDK. A first query analyzes a payments module and proposes two refactoring strategies, and the service stores that run's session_id. To compare the strategies, the service launches two queries at the same time, each with resume set to that ID and forkSession: true, one told to implement strategy A and one strategy B. Both use the service's single checkout of the repository as cwd, with permissionMode "acceptEdits". The two forks report different session IDs and their transcripts look clean, but the diff collected for strategy B contains strategy A's edits, and the test suite fails for both. The original session must stay usable for a later follow-up. What change fixes the comparison?

options.text: Drop forkSession and resume the original session ID in both queries, so each strategy builds directly on the stored analysis instead of on a copy of it.
options.rationale: Wrong. Resuming without forking adds both runs to the original session's history, which the service needs to keep intact, and the two runs still edit the same files.

options.text: Enable file checkpointing on both forks and rewind each one to its first checkpoint whenever its diff shows edits that the other strategy made.
options.rationale: Wrong. Rewinding restores files after the fact; it cannot stop two forks running at once in one directory from overwriting each other mid-run, and edits made through Bash are not tracked.

options.text: Give each fork its own working copy of the repository, such as a separate git worktree, as its cwd, and keep resume with forkSession.
options.rationale: Correct. A fork copies the conversation history, not the filesystem, so a forked agent's edits are real and visible to every session in the same directory; separate working copies keep the strategies apart while each fork keeps the analysis.

options.text: Switch both queries to continue: true so the SDK picks up the analysis session automatically, without the service tracking or passing any session IDs.
options.rationale: Wrong. continue resumes the most recent session in the directory and adds to it rather than forking, and it does nothing to separate the two strategies' file changes.

questions.explanation: Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem, and forking branches only the history: a forked agent's edits land on disk for every session sharing that directory. Parallel experiments need separate working directories; file checkpointing rewinds one session's tracked edits and does not isolate concurrent runs.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the Agent SDK sessions page: fork creates a new session with a copy of the original's history and leaves the original unchanged; forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem, and a forked agent's edits are real and visible to any session working in the same directory; continue finds the most recent session in the current directory. The file-checkpointing page confirms only Write, Edit and NotebookEdit changes are tracked (not Bash), checkpoints are tied to the session that created them, and rewinding restores files on disk. Resuming from a worktree cwd works: the CLI sessions page says resume looks in the current project directory and its git worktrees first, then every other project on the machine, and before v2.1.223 it stopped at the current project directory and its git worktrees, so a git worktree of the same repository resolves either way. A sessionStore adapter keys lookups on cwd, but this scenario does not use one.

questions.stem: An internal "repo doctor" assistant runs on the TypeScript Agent SDK and delegates log triage and dependency audits to two custom subagents. Users complained that long runs looked frozen, because the web UI rendered only AssistantMessage objects, which arrive only after Claude finishes generating each response. The team set includePartialMessages: true and built a live view: a main pane that appends text_delta chunks from stream_event messages, and one pane per subagent that shows the stream events whose parent_tool_use_id matches that subagent's Agent tool call. The main pane now streams smoothly, but both subagent panes stay empty for the whole run, even though the final result shows that both subagents finished their work. What should the team change?

options.text: Fill each subagent pane from complete messages whose parent_tool_use_id matches, such as its tool calls and results, and stream tokens only in the main pane.
options.rationale: Correct. Stream events cover the main session only, with parent_tool_use_id always null, while complete messages from inside a subagent carry parent_tool_use_id, which is the documented way to attribute output to a subagent.

options.text: Turn on partial messages for each subagent as well, through its AgentDefinition, so the subagents emit their own stream_event messages with parent_tool_use_id set.
options.rationale: Wrong. AgentDefinition has no such field, and stream events are emitted for the main session only: token-level deltas from subagents are not forwarded.

options.text: Key each subagent pane on the stream event's session_id instead, since every subagent streams its tokens under a session ID of its own.
options.rationale: Wrong. No key can fix this: stream events are emitted for the main session only, so a subagent's token deltas never reach the stream to be matched.

options.text: Replace the subagents with parallel tool calls in the main agent, because subagent work cannot be observed until the subagent returns its final message.
options.rationale: Wrong. Messages from inside a subagent already reach the stream with parent_tool_use_id set, and folding the work into the main agent gives up the context isolation that keeps the main conversation small.

questions.explanation: With partial messages on, StreamEvent carries raw API events for the main session only, so its parent_tool_use_id is always null. Attribute work to subagents with complete messages, which carry parent_tool_use_id, and reserve token-level rendering for the main agent.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the streaming-output page: by default the SDK yields complete AssistantMessage objects after Claude finishes generating each response; StreamEvent's parent_tool_use_id is always null because stream events are emitted for the main session only and token-level deltas from subagents are not forwarded; to attribute output to a subagent, use complete messages, which carry parent_tool_use_id. The subagents page confirms messages from within a subagent's context include parent_tool_use_id and lists the AgentDefinition fields (no partial-message field). The headless page says the stream carries a subagent's tool_use and tool_result blocks by default and its text and thinking only with --forward-subagent-text, so the key cites tool calls and results. Option c was rewritten to drop a claim about user_message_uuid that could not be confirmed on a fetched page. Volatile because it rests on a documented streaming limitation that could change in a later SDK release.

questions.stem: A nightly GitHub Actions job runs a Python script that calls the Agent SDK's query() with max_turns=40 to triage the day's failing tests and post a summary to the team channel. The script wraps the loop in try/except, logs any exception as a warning, posts the text of the last AssistantMessage it received, and exits 0. Last week the channel got a half-finished summary from a run that hit the turn limit while the job showed green, and on another night the model refused partway through the final turn, yet the post read like a normal report. The leads want the pipeline to post only finished triage, fail visibly when the loop stops early, and send refused runs to a person. Which TWO changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Branch on the ResultMessage subtype: post its result field only on success, and fail the job with the subtype logged for error subtypes such as error_max_turns.
options.rationale: Correct. The subtype is the documented way to tell whether the loop finished or stopped on a limit or an error, and the result field is present only on the success subtype.

options.text: Post the ResultMessage's result field whatever its subtype is, since every subtype carries the final text along with total_cost_usd, usage and session_id.
options.rationale: Wrong. Every subtype carries total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id, but the result text is present only on the success subtype.

options.text: Also check the stop_reason of the run's final turn, and when it is "refusal", route the run to a person instead of posting it as a report.
options.rationale: Correct. The ResultMessage carries the final turn's stop_reason, and the documented way to detect a refusal is to check it for "refusal"; a refusal is a normal response, not an API error.

options.text: Treat a run whose last AssistantMessage contains text as finished, since the loop only writes text to the user on its final turn, and post that text as the report.
options.rationale: Wrong. Claude can return text alongside tool calls on any turn, so a run that hit the turn limit can still end on a message with text; the documented signal for how the loop ended is the ResultMessage subtype.

options.text: Raise max_turns to 200 so every run finishes the triage instead of stopping early, and keep posting the last AssistantMessage text as the report.
options.rationale: Wrong. A higher limit makes the turn limit rarer, but the loop can still end in error_during_execution or a refusal, and the script still posts whatever text came last without knowing which outcome occurred.

questions.explanation: The ResultMessage subtype reports how the agent loop ended: only success carries the result text, while error subtypes such as error_max_turns and error_during_execution should fail the job instead of posting. Its stop_reason says why the model stopped on the final turn, and a refusal arrives as a normal response, so check for "refusal" and send those runs to a person.
questions.verification_note: Rewritten in the verify pass so neither key tests budget caps (d1-024) or session resume (d3-019). Confirmed on the agent-loop page: the ResultMessage subtype (success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution, error_max_structured_output_retries) is the primary way to check termination state; the result field is present only on success; all subtypes carry total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id; a single-shot query() yields the error result and then raises; Claude may respond with text, tool calls, or both on a turn; the result's stop_reason gives why the model stopped on its final turn, and refusals are detected by checking stop_reason for "refusal". The handling-stop-reasons page confirms a refusal is returned as a normal HTTP 200 response, not an error. Key c is phrased around the final turn's stop_reason, a durable concept, rather than resting on the ResultMessage field name.

questions.stem: A research platform's literature worker calls the Messages API in a hand-written loop with two client tools, search_papers and fetch_paper. After a refactor meant to cut latency, the loop appends each tool_result to the history as its own user message, in the order the calls finish. Since then, Claude issues one tool call per turn instead of the four or five parallel searches it used to make, and runs take far longer. Separately, when fetch_paper hits a paywall, the loop returns the bare string "failed" as ordinary result content, and Claude usually drops the paper instead of looking for an open-access copy. The model and prompts have not changed. Which TWO changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so Claude must call a tool on every turn, which pushes it back toward batching several searches into one response.
options.rationale: Wrong. Forcing a tool call does nothing about the split-message history that suppressed parallel calls, and current models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1) do not support the any or tool types.

options.text: Return all tool_result blocks for an assistant turn together in the next user message, each matched by tool_use_id and placed before any text.
options.rationale: Correct. Formatting results incorrectly, such as in separate user messages, is the most common cause of lost parallelism, because that history teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls.

options.text: Leave failed fetch_paper calls out of the next user message so Claude sees only successful results and is not distracted by paywall errors.
options.rationale: Wrong. Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result; leaving one out makes the request fail with an error about missing tool_result blocks.

options.text: Add disable_parallel_tool_use: false to tool_choice on each request so the API switches parallel calls back on after the model turned them off.
options.rationale: Wrong. Parallel calls are already allowed by default and nothing switched them off; the cause is the conversation history the refactored loop builds.

options.text: Return paywall failures with is_error: true and a message that names the paywall and suggests searching for an arXiv or open-access copy.
options.rationale: Correct. is_error marks the call as failed, and the docs recommend errors that say what went wrong and what Claude should try next instead of a generic failure string.

questions.explanation: Claude learns from the history you send: results split across several user messages teach it to stop making parallel calls, so return every result for a turn in one user message. Failures belong in a tool_result with is_error: true and an instructive message, never dropped from the history.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the parallel-tool-use page: return one tool_result per tool_use, all together in the next user message, before any text; separate user messages teach Claude to avoid parallel calls; parallel calls are on by default. The handle-tool-calls page covers is_error and instructive error messages, and the stop-reasons page says a missing tool_result fails with an error about missing blocks. The parallel page notes Fable 5.1 may issue fewer parallel calls in long agent loops; the stem rules this out by saying the model is unchanged and the drop began with the refactor. Drift: current docs say Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 do not support tool_choice any or tool (a 400 on the newest models), while exam-era material may treat forcing as merely unhelpful; option a is wrong in either era.

questions.stem: In an Agent SDK agent, Claude often requests several calls to your custom lookup_sku tool in one turn, but they always run one after another. The tool only reads data. What lets those calls run concurrently?

options.text: Add lookup_sku to allowedTools so its calls skip the approval step and execute in parallel.
options.rationale: Wrong. allowedTools only auto-approves calls; custom tools still default to sequential execution.

options.text: Set readOnlyHint in the tool's annotations so the SDK can schedule its calls concurrently.
options.rationale: Correct. Custom tools run sequentially by default, and setting readOnlyHint in their annotations lets the SDK run them concurrently like built-in read-only tools.

options.text: Set disable_parallel_tool_use to false in the query's tool_choice.
options.rationale: Wrong. That Messages API setting governs whether Claude requests several tools in one response, which it already does; it does not change how the SDK executes them.

options.text: State in the tool description that it is read-only and safe to call in parallel.
options.rationale: Wrong. A description steers Claude's choices but does not change the SDK's execution strategy, which reads the readOnlyHint annotation.

questions.explanation: When Claude requests several tools in one turn, the Agent SDK can run read-only tools (Read, Glob, Grep, MCP tools marked read-only) concurrently and state-changing tools such as Edit, Write and Bash sequentially. Custom tools are sequential unless their annotations set readOnlyHint.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the agent-loop page (Parallel tool execution): read-only tools can run concurrently, state-modifying tools run sequentially, custom tools default to sequential, and setting readOnlyHint in the tool's annotations enables parallel execution (field name taken from the MCP SDK). Volatile because the key rests on an annotation name.

questions.stem: A Messages API response arrives with stop_reason "model_context_window_exceeded". What should your code conclude?

options.text: The input was too long, so nothing was generated; shorten the prompt and resend.
options.rationale: Wrong. Stop reasons arrive on successful responses; this one means Claude generated output until the context window filled.

options.text: The max_tokens value you set was reached; raise max_tokens and retry the request.
options.rationale: Wrong. That is the max_tokens stop reason; here the model's context window, not your max_tokens setting, ended generation.

options.text: Generation hit the model's context window limit; treat the output as valid but truncated.
options.rationale: Correct. Claude stopped because it reached the context window limit, which lets you request maximum tokens without computing input size; the response is valid but truncated.

options.text: The server-side tool loop hit its iteration limit; send the response back unchanged to continue.
options.rationale: Wrong. That describes pause_turn, which applies only to server tools such as web search.

questions.explanation: model_context_window_exceeded means output filled the remaining context window, so the response is usable but cut short and should be handled like other truncation. It lets you set a large max_tokens without calculating input size, and like every stop reason it comes on a successful response, not as a 4xx or 5xx error.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the handling-stop-reasons page: the stop reason table says model_context_window_exceeded means Claude filled the model's context window and should be treated as truncated, it lets you request maximum tokens without knowing input size, and stop reasons are HTTP 200 successes distinct from 4xx/5xx errors. On Sonnet 4.5 and newer models the API returns it without a beta header; earlier models need the model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26 header, and the SDKs type it only in the beta namespace. The key does not rest on those details.

questions.stem: A Python service that answers a waiting user calls client.messages.create() with max_tokens=128000, and the SDK refuses the non-streaming request as likely to exceed 10 minutes. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Call client.messages.stream() and use get_final_message() to get the complete Message.
options.rationale: Correct. Streaming keeps the connection alive with server-sent events, and get_final_message() accumulates them into the same Message object create() returns.

options.text: Submit the request through the Message Batches API and return the result once its batch finishes.
options.rationale: Wrong. Batches suit long jobs that can poll for results later, not a user waiting on a live answer.

options.text: Lower max_tokens to 4096 and keep sending continuation requests on each max_tokens stop.
options.rationale: Wrong. This trades one request for many and leaves you stitching partial outputs together, when streaming handles the long request directly.

options.text: Pass stream=True to create() and read the full Message from the final message_stop event.
options.rationale: Wrong. The message_stop event carries no Message, and message_start's Message has empty content; the content arrives as deltas that you would have to accumulate yourself.

questions.explanation: The SDKs reject non-streaming requests expected to exceed the 10-minute timeout, so large max_tokens values need streaming. If you do not need incremental text, stream anyway and call get_final_message() to receive the same Message object; keep the Batches API for work that can poll for results.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the streaming page: the SDK requires streaming for large max_tokens values to avoid HTTP timeouts, get_final_message() collects the events into a Message identical to what create() returns, and message_start carries a Message with empty content followed by content block events. The errors page says the SDKs validate that non-streaming requests are not expected to exceed a 10-minute timeout and recommends streaming or the Batches API (which you poll) for long requests. Volatile because the key rests on the 10-minute limit.

questions.stem: A consulting firm's research assistant runs one Claude agent with web search for every request. The team piloted an orchestrator-worker version, a lead agent that delegates to parallel research subagents, on three request types. On broad market scans, such as profiling 15 competitors across pricing, funding, and hiring, the pilot scored clearly higher on the team's eval set, and analysts say the reports justify the extra spend. On single-fact lookups from the in-app quick-answer box, accuracy was unchanged while token use and cost rose about tenfold and p95 latency went from 6 to 40 seconds. On contract cross-referencing, where every step depends on the findings of the step before and all reasoning needs the same set of clauses, which fits easily in one context window, the pilot scored lower than the single agent. Leadership wants one rollout decision. What should the team do?

options.text: Roll out the multi-agent design for all three request types, but run every subagent on a smaller, cheaper model so the added token spend on lookups and contract work is offset.
options.rationale: Cheaper subagents trim spend but keep the fan-out latency on lookups and the contract regression. Anthropic flags work that needs shared context or has many dependencies between agents as a poor fit for multi-agent systems today.

options.text: Roll out the multi-agent design for all three types and switch the subagents to asynchronous execution, so the lead agent stops waiting on slow subagents and lookups get faster.
options.rationale: Anthropic's research system runs subagents synchronously and notes that asynchronous execution adds challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation. It also does nothing about fan-out token cost on lookups or the contract regression.

options.text: Use the multi-agent design only for broad market scans, and keep the single agent for quick lookups and contract cross-referencing, where delegation adds cost without a gain.
options.rationale: Multi-agent research excels on breadth-first queries that pursue independent directions, when the task's value covers far higher token use (about 15 times a chat in Anthropic's system). Lookups and dependent, shared-context work pay that cost and latency with no gain, so they stay on the simpler design.

options.text: Use the multi-agent design for contract cross-referencing and market scans, since those are the hardest request types, and keep the single agent only for quick-answer lookups.
options.rationale: Difficulty alone does not make a task a good fit. Work where each step depends on the last and every agent needs the same context is exactly the case Anthropic calls a poor fit, which matches the pilot's lower score.

questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems trade much higher token use for better results on breadth-first, parallelizable work, so use them where the task's value covers that cost. Single-fact lookups and tightly dependent, shared-context work do not benefit: when work is one dependent chain or fits in one context, an orchestrator pays for a plan, a handoff, and a merge that a single model gets for free.
questions.verification_note: The 2026 cost guide says an orchestrator saved money in only two measured situations: capping a cost tail on routine work, and input larger than one context window. The stem rules out both: the single agent shows no cost tail on lookups (p95 of 6 seconds) and delegation raised lookup cost tenfold, and the contract work is one dependent chain that fits in one context window. The key holds under both the 2025 engineering post and the 2026 guide.

questions.stem: An accounts-payable platform extracts fields from uploaded documents into JSON using one Claude prompt with a tool schema. Uploads are a mix of supplier invoices, credit memos, and bank remittance advices, each with different required fields and layout quirks. Over three months the team kept adding invoice-specific instructions and examples to fix invoice errors. Invoice accuracy rose, but remittance extraction regressed after each change, and the prompt is now 9,000 tokens, most of it irrelevant to any single document. A quick test showed that document type can be identified from the first page with over 99% accuracy. Throughput and cost both matter, because the platform processes 80,000 documents a day. Which redesign best addresses the regression?

options.text: Classify each upload by document type first, then send it to a type-specific extraction prompt and schema, so tuning one type no longer affects the others.
options.rationale: This is routing: distinct categories that are better handled separately, with a classification step that an LLM or a traditional classifier can do accurately. Separate prompts stop optimization for one input type from hurting the others and keep each prompt short.

options.text: Keep the single prompt and add an evaluator call that scores each extraction against the schema and reruns extraction with feedback until the score passes.
options.rationale: An evaluator-optimizer loop adds at least one extra call per document and still sends every type through the same conflicted prompt. That pattern suits clear criteria where iterative refinement adds measurable value, not a structural conflict between input types.

options.text: Run the single prompt three times on every document and keep only the field values that at least two runs agree on, filtering out type-specific mistakes.
options.rationale: Voting raises confidence by sampling the same task several times, but runs of one prompt share its systematic bias against remittances. It also triples extraction cost at 80,000 documents a day.

options.text: Add an orchestrator that reads each document, decides which extraction subtasks it needs, and dispatches worker calls for each field group before merging results.
options.rationale: Orchestrator-workers fits tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. Here the document types are known and classifiable, so dynamic planning adds calls and latency where a simple router suffices.

questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up prompt, which matters when optimizing for one kind of input hurts performance on others. When categories are distinct and classification is reliable, a router is simpler and cheaper than voting, refinement loops, or dynamic orchestration.

questions.stem: A SaaS company wants Claude to draft first replies to support tickets about documented product features. Support staff review every draft before it is sent, and the assistant takes no actions on customer accounts. An engineer built a prototype in which a planner agent spawns researcher subagents to search the help center, a writer drafts the reply, and a critic loops with the writer until it approves. On a 300-ticket eval set graded by the support leads, the prototype scored 87%, against 86% for a baseline that makes one Claude call with the top five retrieved help-center articles and four example replies in the prompt. The prototype costs about 12 times more per ticket and takes 45 seconds per draft instead of 5. What should the team ship?

options.text: The prototype, with smaller models for the researcher subagents and the critic, which brings the per-ticket cost close to the baseline while keeping its one-point lead.
options.rationale: Smaller models trim cost but keep the extra calls, the added latency, and the moving parts, all for a lead of about three tickets out of 300. Complexity should be added only when it is shown to be needed.

options.text: The prototype unchanged, because token usage explains most of the variance in agent performance, so the larger token spend is what keeps quality up as volume grows.
options.rationale: That finding comes from Anthropic's evaluation of a browsing research system on BrowseComp. It does not mean more tokens help a retrieval-grounded drafting task, and the team's own eval shows no meaningful gain.

options.text: A single autonomous agent with search tools that decides its own steps for each ticket, which avoids multi-agent overhead while keeping flexibility for unusual tickets.
options.rationale: Agents suit open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted and a fixed path cannot be hardcoded. Drafting from retrieved help articles follows a known path, so autonomy adds cost and the risk of compounding errors without a benefit.

options.text: The baseline single call with retrieval and examples, adding a step such as a critic later only if evals on real tickets show a gap that the step closes.
options.rationale: Anthropic advises finding the simplest solution and increasing complexity only when needed, noting that a single LLM call optimized with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough for many applications. The eval set then shows when an added step earns its cost.

questions.explanation: Start with the simplest design that meets the bar: for many applications, one LLM call with retrieval and in-context examples is enough. Agentic and multi-agent designs trade latency and cost for performance, so adopt them only when evals show the gain is worth that trade.

questions.stem: Your platform team is building an internal pull request reviewer that calls the Messages API directly from a webhook service. Every PR gets the same three fixed checks: security vulnerabilities, missing tests, and documentation gaps. The checks do not depend on each other's results. Missing a real vulnerability is expensive for the company, and the current single security prompt is inconsistent: it flags an injection risk on one run and misses it on the next run of the same diff. A false alarm only costs a reviewer a minute. Engineers want the review comment posted within about a minute of opening the PR, so long serial pipelines are a problem. Which TWO design choices best fit these requirements? Select TWO.

options.text: Use an orchestrator LLM that reads each diff and decides which review subtasks to create, then delegates them to worker calls and synthesizes the findings.
options.rationale: Orchestrator-workers is for tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. These three checks are fixed for every PR, so the planning and synthesis calls add latency and cost where simpler parallelization does the job.

options.text: Run the security, test, and documentation checks as separate parallel calls, each with its own focused prompt, then merge their findings into one comment.
options.rationale: This is sectioning: independent subtasks run in parallel for speed. LLMs generally perform better when each consideration gets its own call, and parallel calls keep the review inside the latency target.

options.text: Chain the checks so each call receives the previous call's findings, letting later checks build on what earlier checks found before the review is posted.
options.rationale: Prompt chaining suits tasks that decompose into dependent fixed steps. These checks are independent, so a chain adds serial latency without improving any check.

options.text: Combine all three checks into one call with detailed instructions for each, since one call sees the whole diff at once and avoids merging separate outputs.
options.rationale: For complex tasks with several considerations, LLMs generally perform better when each consideration is handled by a separate call. Crowding all three checks into one prompt splits attention further when the security check is already inconsistent on its own.

options.text: Run several differently worded security prompts on each diff with a low vote threshold, flagging the code if even one or two of them report a problem.
options.rationale: This is voting: several prompts review the same code for higher-confidence results. Vote thresholds balance false positives against false negatives, and a low threshold fits here because a missed vulnerability costs far more than a false alarm.

questions.explanation: Parallelization has two forms: sectioning splits independent subtasks into separate calls that run at once, and voting runs the same task several times for higher confidence. Fixed, independent checks call for sectioning rather than an orchestrator or a chain, and an inconsistent high-stakes check benefits from voting with a threshold tuned to the cost of each kind of error.

questions.stem: A coding assistant must change however many files each feature request needs, and nobody can list those files in advance. Why is orchestrator-workers a better fit than sectioning?

options.text: Orchestrator-workers runs all of its worker calls in parallel, while sectioning has to run its subtasks one after another.
options.rationale: Sectioning is defined as breaking a task into independent subtasks that run in parallel, so parallelism does not separate the two.

options.text: The orchestrator works out the subtasks from the specific request, while sectioning needs its subtasks defined in advance.
options.rationale: Correct. The key difference from parallelization is flexibility: subtasks are not predefined but determined by the orchestrator based on the input, which is why coding changes across an unknown set of files fit it.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers samples every file edit several times and keeps the majority answer, which sectioning cannot do.
options.rationale: Running the same task several times and aggregating is voting, the other form of parallelization, not orchestrator-workers.

options.text: Orchestrator-workers makes fewer model calls than sectioning, so it costs less as the file count grows.
options.rationale: The pattern does not save calls: it adds an orchestrator call to plan the subtasks, and the cookbook implementation makes one orchestrator call plus one call per worker.

questions.explanation: Use orchestrator-workers when the subtasks depend on the input and cannot be listed ahead of time. When the subtasks are predictable, plain sectioning is simpler and cheaper.

questions.stem: A prompt chain writes a document outline, then drafts the document from that outline. What does a programmatic gate between those two steps do?

options.text: It caches the outline so the drafting call can reuse it at a lower price per input token.
options.rationale: That describes prompt caching, which lowers the cost of repeated prefixes. It does not check whether the chain is still on track.

options.text: It sends the outline to a second model that rewrites it in a loop until a judge approves it.
options.rationale: A generate, critique, and revise loop is the evaluator-optimizer pattern. A gate is a programmatic check, not another model loop.

options.text: It runs the outline step and the drafting step at the same time so the chain finishes sooner.
options.rationale: A chain is sequential by design because each call processes the previous call's output. Running steps at once is parallelization.

options.text: It checks the outline in code against set criteria before the drafting step runs.
options.rationale: Correct. Programmatic checks on intermediate steps keep the process on track, as in checking that an outline meets certain criteria before writing the document.

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining trades latency for accuracy by making each call an easier task, and gates are code checks on intermediate steps that keep the process on track, catching a bad outline before the draft is built on it.

questions.stem: Which condition best signals that a task is a good fit for an evaluator-optimizer loop rather than a different workflow pattern?

options.text: Clear evaluation criteria exist, and LLM feedback can measurably improve each new draft.
options.rationale: Correct. Evaluator-optimizer is particularly effective with clear criteria and when iterative refinement adds measurable value: responses improve with articulated feedback, and an LLM can provide that feedback.

options.text: Inputs fall into distinct categories, and each category needs its own specialized prompt.
options.rationale: Distinct categories that are better handled separately are the signal for routing.

options.text: The needed subtasks cannot be predicted until the specific input has been examined.
options.rationale: Subtasks that depend on the input and cannot be predicted are the signal for orchestrator-workers.

options.text: The work splits into independent subtasks that can all run at the same time for speed.
options.rationale: Independent subtasks run in parallel for speed are the signal for sectioning, one form of parallelization.

questions.explanation: Each workflow pattern has its own fit signal. Evaluator-optimizer pays off when there are clear criteria for judging output and feedback measurably improves it, much like a writer revising a draft after critique.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a release agent built on the Claude Agent SDK (TypeScript) inside a GitHub Actions job. After each merge it writes a database migration and runs `./scripts/migrate --env prod`, which cannot be undone. Policy requires a DBA to approve every production migration, and DBAs often answer hours later. Runners are billed per minute and jobs are killed after 60 minutes. After approval, the agent must continue in the same session so it can run post-migration checks and write release notes from what it already learned. Today the job lists Bash in allowedTools and relies on a system prompt rule telling Claude to wait for a DBA reply in Slack, a step Claude sometimes skips. Which design best gates the migration?

options.text: Remove Bash from allowedTools and add a canUseTool callback that posts the migrate command to the DBA channel in Slack and awaits the reply before returning allow or deny, keeping the session open in the job until a DBA answers the thread.
options.rationale: Wrong. The callback can stay pending indefinitely and the run stays paused while it waits, so the runner keeps billing and the 60-minute kill ends the job with the approval outstanding; the docs recommend a defer hook when a person may take longer than the process can stay running.

options.text: Set permissionMode to "dontAsk" and leave the migrate command out of every allow rule, so the call is denied automatically and Claude reports in its result that a DBA must approve the migration before anyone reruns the job.
options.rationale: Wrong. dontAsk turns the call into a denial without ever invoking canUseTool, so nothing is held for a DBA to approve; Claude only learns the call was refused, and a rerun starts a new session that is denied the same way.

options.text: Add a PreToolUse hook that returns "defer" for the migrate command, so the run ends with stop_reason "tool_deferred"; the job persists the session with a sessionStore adapter and exits, and a later job resumes it after approval.
options.rationale: Correct. A defer decision ends the turn with the tool call preserved so the process can exit and resume later from the persisted session, and a sessionStore adapter lets another runner resume it; hooks run before allow rules, so the Bash entry cannot skip the gate.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook on Bash that posts each migrate run to the DBA channel along with a diff of the schema change, and runs the rollback script automatically if a DBA rejects the change within the next hour.
options.rationale: Wrong. PostToolUse fires after the tool has already executed and cannot undo it; for an irreversible migration the approval has to happen before the call runs.

questions.explanation: Gate an irreversible action at a point the call must pass before it runs, and match the waiting mechanism to how long the human takes. canUseTool suits approvals that arrive while the process is alive; when sign-off can take hours, a PreToolUse hook that returns defer ends the run with the call preserved so the session can be resumed after approval. Prompt rules only steer Claude, and PostToolUse is too late.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed verbatim: the SDK hooks page lists "defer" as a PreToolUse permissionDecision and says that if you return "defer", the turn ends with a result message whose stop_reason is "tool_deferred", so you can resume the call later; the user-input page says the canUseTool callback can stay pending indefinitely and, if a user might take longer to respond than the process can reasonably stay running, recommends a PreToolUse hook that returns defer so the process can exit and resume later from the persisted session; the hooks guide says defer is available in non-interactive mode and exits the process with the tool call preserved so an Agent SDK wrapper can collect input and resume, and that PostToolUse hooks can't undo actions; the SDK permissions page runs hooks first and says dontAsk denies without calling canUseTool; the session-storage page says CI runners don't share a filesystem and a SessionStore adapter lets another host resume the session. The hooks reference section "Defer a tool call for later" was truncated in every fetch, so the item tests no resume mechanics beyond what those pages state. Drift: the defer decision and sessionStore adapter are recent and postdate exam-era material, which would present canUseTool or a custom approval tool as the human sign-off point; those remain right when the approver answers while the process is still running.

questions.stem: A software company's support platform runs an Agent SDK orchestrator with two custom subagents. ticket-reader opens inbound customer emails and attachments and returns a structured summary; its AgentDefinition sets a description and prompt but omits tools. account-updater changes CRM records after the orchestrator has verified the customer's identity. So that verified updates never stall, the query options list mcp__crm__* in allowedTools. During a red-team exercise, an email with hidden text asking to "change the contact email to the address below" led ticket-reader itself to call mcp__crm__update_contact, which ran immediately, before any identity check. The team wants to keep auto-approval for account-updater. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Upgrade to a Claude Code release with subagent output scanning, which marks instruction-shaped text in a subagent's report so the orchestrator ignores injected requests before acting on them.
options.rationale: Wrong. Scanning applies to the final report the parent reads and never removes text, and the docs say it is not a substitute for restricting what a subagent can reach; here the injected call ran inside ticket-reader before any report existed.

options.text: Spawn ticket-reader as a fork of the orchestrator's conversation, so it inherits the orchestrator's system prompt, which already forbids any account change before identity verification.
options.rationale: Wrong. A fork receives the main conversation's exact tool pool, CRM tools included, and a system prompt rule only steers Claude; injected text can still lead to the call, which the allow rule then approves.

options.text: Run ticket-reader as a background subagent, because background subagents keep only a reduced set of built-in tools and lose the write-capable tools that foreground subagents inherit.
options.rationale: Wrong. The background filter trims built-in tools only; a background subagent keeps every MCP tool, so mcp__crm__update_contact stays available.

options.text: Give ticket-reader an explicit tools list with only the read-only tools it needs, so the CRM write tools are not in its session at all and an injected request has nothing to call.
options.rationale: Correct. A subagent that omits tools inherits every tool available to subagents, and subagents inherit the parent's permission rules; a tool left out of its tools list is not in its session at all, so the injection cannot trigger the write.

questions.explanation: Least privilege is a subagent's real safety boundary: an agent that reads untrusted content should not hold tools that can act on it. Listing tools on the AgentDefinition removes everything else from that subagent's session, while auto-approval stays in place for the subagent that needs the write tool. Output scanning, prompt rules and background mode do not narrow what the reader can call.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the SDK subagents page says an omitted tools field inherits every tool available to subagents and that a tool you leave out isn't in the subagent's session at all; the sub-agents page says forks receive the main conversation's exact tool pool, a background subagent keeps every MCP tool while losing some built-ins, and output scanning never removes or rewords anything and isn't a substitute for restricting what a subagent can reach; the SDK hooks page says subagents inherit permission rules from the parent conversation; the SDK permissions page says mcp__<server>__* allow rules match every tool from that server. Drift: background-by-default subagents (Claude Code v2.1.198) and output scanning (v2.1.210) are recent behavior that exam-era material may not mention; the key (a tools allowlist for the subagent that reads untrusted content) is a durable least-privilege principle and does not depend on them.

questions.stem: A developer is on a local feature branch with six unpushed commits that add a new payments module. They ask Claude Code to write tests for four independent services in that module, and Claude spawns four background subagents from a custom test-writer definition in .claude/agents/. Each subagent edits files and runs the test suite. The runs are flaky: one subagent's half-written fixture breaks another's test run, and two subagents overwrite each other's change to a shared test helper. The developer wants the work to stay parallel and each subagent's changes kept apart for review. No settings file configures worktrees. What is the best change?

options.text: Add isolation: worktree to the test-writer frontmatter, so each subagent edits files and runs its tests in its own temporary git worktree, with its own files and branch.
options.rationale: Wrong. This isolates the edits, but subagent worktrees branch from the repository's default branch on the remote unless worktree.baseRef is "head", so the subagents would not see the six unpushed commits that add the payments module.

options.text: Add isolation: worktree to the test-writer frontmatter and set worktree.baseRef to "head" in settings, so each subagent's worktree branches from the current local HEAD.
options.rationale: Correct. Each subagent gets its own worktree, so parallel edits and test runs stop colliding and each set of changes stays separate, and the head base carries the unpushed feature-branch commits the new tests depend on.

options.text: Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS to 1 so only one test-writer runs against the checkout at a time, and have each subagent commit its tests before the next one starts.
options.rationale: Wrong. At the limit Claude Code refuses further spawns, so this serializes the work the developer wants parallel, and all four sets of changes still land in the same checkout.

options.text: Keep the subagents in the main checkout but give each a delegation prompt that lists the files it owns and tells it never to edit shared helpers or fixtures another subagent may need.
options.rationale: Wrong. Prompt boundaries only steer; the subagents still share one working tree, so test runs see each other's in-progress edits and the changes are not kept apart.

questions.explanation: Parallel subagents that edit and test in one checkout interfere with each other, and isolation: worktree gives each one its own working directory and branch. Worktrees branch from the remote default branch by default, so when subagents must build on unpushed local work, set worktree.baseRef to "head". Serializing the subagents or writing prompt boundaries either gives up parallelism or isolates nothing.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the worktrees page says subagents can run in their own worktrees so parallel edits don't conflict, that a worktree has its own files and branch, that subagent worktrees use the same base branch as --worktree and branch from the repository's default branch unless worktree.baseRef is "head", that "fresh" (the default) branches from the default branch on the remote, and that "head" carries unpushed commits and is meant for isolating subagents that need to operate on in-progress work; the sub-agents page documents isolation: worktree in frontmatter, branched by default from the default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD; the SDK subagents page says the concurrency limit refuses further spawns. Drift: worktree.baseRef is recent; exam-era material may present isolation: worktree on its own as the complete answer, which is option a here.

questions.stem: A market-research product runs its lead agent on Claude Opus 5 through the TypeScript Agent SDK with a custom systemPrompt. Since the model upgrade, broad questions fan out into trees of subagents that spawn subagents of their own; one query ran for 40 minutes and cost $63. Answers are still good, so the team wants to keep delegation. Finance wants hard limits on how deep and wide a query can fan out and on what it can spend, enforced by the runtime no matter how Claude decides to delegate. The options set allowedTools to Read, WebSearch, WebFetch and Agent, and maxTurns to 40, with no other limits. Which TWO changes enforce those limits? Select TWO.

options.text: Add the Opus 5 prompting guide's delegation instruction to the custom systemPrompt, so Claude spawns subagents only when a question really needs them and handles simple lookups itself.
options.rationale: Wrong. The docs say this instruction, like the line the claude_code preset adds for Opus 5, only steers Claude; it can reduce fan-out but enforces no limit.

options.text: Set maxBudgetUsd on the query; subagent requests count toward it, and at the cap Claude Code refuses new spawns, stops running background subagents and ends with error_max_budget_usd.
options.rationale: Correct. The spend cap covers the whole query, subagent requests included, and Claude Code enforces it however Claude decides to delegate.

options.text: Set model to "haiku" in every AgentDefinition, so each subagent request costs a fraction of an Opus 5 request and a fanned-out query can no longer approach the $63 run.
options.rationale: Wrong. A cheaper subagent model lowers the cost of each request but adds no limit: it changes neither how deep or wide the tree can grow nor what the whole query may spend.

options.text: Lower maxTurns from 40 to 10, since maxTurns counts every tool call the query makes, subagents included, so ten calls bound the size of the whole agent tree.
options.rationale: Wrong. maxTurns counts tool-use round trips, not tool calls, and one turn can launch several subagents at once; it sets no bound on nesting depth or spend, which is why the docs give depth, concurrency and spend as the caps for a subagent tree.

options.text: Pass CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1 and a low CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS through the env option, spreading process.env, so subagents cannot nest and few run at once.
options.rationale: Correct. Depth 1 stops subagents from spawning their own, the concurrency limit refuses spawns past the cap, and the TypeScript SDK replaces the subprocess environment with env, so process.env has to be spread in.

questions.explanation: Delegation instructions only steer the model. To bound a subagent tree, use the limits Claude Code enforces: maxBudgetUsd for whole-query spend, subagents included, and the spawn-depth and concurrency limits for the tree's shape. A cheaper subagent model or a lower maxTurns changes cost or pacing but caps neither the tree nor its spend.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the SDK subagents page lists depth (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH, 1 stops your subagents from spawning their own), concurrency (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS, refuses further spawns) and spend (maxBudgetUsd, compared against total_cost_usd so subagent requests count) as the three caps, describes the budget cap's three enforcement behaviors (refuses spawns, stops background subagents, ends with error_max_budget_usd), says Opus 5 delegates more readily and that either delegation instruction only steers Claude while Claude Code enforces the limits however Claude delegates, says the TypeScript env option replaces the subprocess environment, and lists model as an AgentDefinition field; the agent-loop page says maxTurns counts tool-use round trips and that one turn can include several tool calls. Option c was rewritten because the SDK subagents troubleshooting section says Agent calls missing from allowedTools fall through to canUseTool, which contradicts the SDK permissions page, so a canUseTool spawn quota was arguable. Drift: the depth and concurrency variables and the budget cap's subagent enforcement require recent releases (Claude Code v2.1.217 to v2.1.219); exam-era material may mention only maxTurns and maxBudgetUsd.

questions.stem: In an Agent SDK app, a custom subagent hits an ambiguous requirement mid-task and needs the user to choose between two database schemas. Which design works?

options.text: The subagent ends with the open question in its final report; the main agent asks the user, then resumes that subagent with the answer.
options.rationale: Correct. AskUserQuestion is not available in subagents, so the question has to travel back in the final report; resuming the subagent by its agentId keeps its full conversation history.

options.text: Add AskUserQuestion to the subagent's tools list so its question reaches the app's canUseTool callback, as it does for the main agent.
options.rationale: Wrong. AskUserQuestion is removed from every subagent, even when it is listed in the tools field.

options.text: Set the subagent's permissionMode to plan, since plan mode is where Claude asks clarifying questions before it proposes any changes.
options.rationale: Wrong. Plan mode lets a subagent keep ExitPlanMode, but AskUserQuestion is still removed from every subagent, so it still cannot ask.

options.text: Run the subagent in the foreground, since a foreground subagent passes its prompts and clarifying questions straight through to the user.
options.rationale: Wrong. Foreground subagents pass permission prompts through, but the filter that removes AskUserQuestion applies to every subagent, foreground or background, so it still cannot ask.

questions.explanation: Only the main agent can ask the user a clarifying question, because AskUserQuestion is filtered out of every subagent. Design subagents to report open questions in their final message, then let the main agent ask and resume the subagent so it keeps its context.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the SDK user-input page says AskUserQuestion is not currently available in subagents spawned via the Agent tool; the sub-agents page says the first tool filter removes AskUserQuestion from every subagent even when listed in tools, keeps ExitPlanMode only when permissionMode is plan, that forks skip the filters, and that foreground subagents pass permission prompts through; the SDK subagents page says a resumed subagent retains its full conversation history and is resumed by its agentId. Drift: exam-era Claude Code subagent docs may have said foreground subagents pass clarifying questions (AskUserQuestion) through to the user, which would make option d look right; current Claude Code docs say only permission prompts pass through, and the SDK user-input page states the subagent limitation directly.

questions.stem: Your Agent SDK app passes a PreToolUse hook in query() options that denies Bash commands containing DROP TABLE. Claude delegates schema work to a custom subagent. Does the guard apply there?

options.text: No. A subagent starts with a fresh context, so the hook has to be registered again for that subagent before its calls are checked.
options.rationale: Wrong. Context isolation covers conversation history; hooks passed in query() options run in your app process and also fire for tool calls made inside subagents.

options.text: Only for foreground subagents; a background subagent's tool calls skip the parent's hooks and follow its permission mode alone.
options.rationale: Wrong. Session hooks fire inside subagents with no foreground or background exception, and hook inputs carry agent_id and agent_type whenever a hook fires inside a subagent.

options.text: Yes. Hooks passed to query() also fire for tool calls made inside subagents, so the same guard checks the subagent's Bash calls.
options.rationale: Correct. Session hooks fire for a subagent's tool calls the same way they do in the main conversation, and the hook input's agent_id and agent_type show which agent made the call.

options.text: Only if the subagent's tools list names Bash explicitly; inherited tools are checked by permission rules but not by hooks.
options.rationale: Wrong. Listing or inheriting Bash only changes which tools the subagent has; any Bash call it makes still passes through PreToolUse.

questions.explanation: Hooks registered on the query are an orchestration-wide guardrail: they fire for tool calls in the main agent and in its subagents. The hook input's agent_id and agent_type let one hook apply different rules per agent.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed: the sub-agents page says session-wide hooks also fire inside subagents and that tool events such as PreToolUse and PostToolUse fire for the subagent's tool calls the same way they do in the main conversation; the SDK hooks page says agent_id and agent_type are populated when the hook fires inside a subagent (in Python as optional fields on PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure and PermissionRequest) and recommends PreToolUse hooks to handle repeated subagent permission prompts. The key no longer depends on the agent_id detail.

questions.stem: In Claude Code, two PreToolUse hooks match the same production deploy command: a policy hook returns "ask" and an auto-approver returns "allow". What happens?

options.text: The command runs with no prompt, since an explicit allow from any matching hook skips the permission prompt.
options.rationale: Wrong. An allow skips the prompt only when no other matching hook returns something more restrictive.

options.text: The user gets a permission prompt, because the most restrictive decision wins and ask outranks allow.
options.rationale: Correct. Claude Code combines PreToolUse decisions most restrictive first, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow, so the ask stands.

options.text: Whichever hook finishes last decides, since matching hooks run in parallel and the final output wins.
options.rationale: Wrong. Last to finish applies when several hooks return updatedInput; permission decisions are combined by restrictiveness.

options.text: The call is denied, because conflicting decisions from matching hooks are treated as a hook error.
options.rationale: Wrong. Conflicts are not errors; ask outranks allow, so the call prompts rather than being denied.

questions.explanation: An approval point built from a PreToolUse ask cannot be overridden by a more permissive hook: Claude Code applies deny, then defer, then ask, then allow. Write each hook to stand on its own, because matching hooks run in parallel in no fixed order.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed verbatim: the hooks guide says that for PreToolUse permission decisions the most restrictive answer applies, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow, that ask shows the permission prompt as normal, that matching hooks run in parallel, and that when multiple PreToolUse hooks return updatedInput the last one to finish takes effect; the SDK hooks page says deny takes priority over defer, which takes priority over ask, which takes priority over allow, and that all matching hooks run in parallel with the most restrictive result applying. The key rests on the long-standing deny over ask over allow precedence; defer is a recent addition that does not change it.

questions.stem: A retail support agent built on the Messages API has two client tools, lookup_order(order_id) and issue_refund(order_id, amount), and Claude often calls lookup_order for several orders in parallel. Three failure types occur in production: the order service occasionally times out, customers mistype order IDs so no match exists, and refunds are blocked by policy once an order is older than 90 days. Today the tool handler catches every exception and returns the plain string "Error" as an ordinary tool_result. Transcripts show Claude telling customers the system is down when they simply mistyped an ID, and calling issue_refund again and again on orders outside the refund window. What change to how the handler reports failures will most improve the agent's behavior?

options.text: Retry every failed call inside the handler up to five times with exponential backoff and jitter, and if it still fails, return a tool_result with is_error: true saying "lookup_order failed, please try again later."
options.rationale: Backoff only helps the timeout case. Retrying a mistyped ID or a policy block cannot succeed, and the final generic message, even flagged with is_error, still gives Claude no way to tell the three failures apart.

options.text: Return each failure as a tool_result with is_error: true and a message giving the cause and next step, such as "Timed out; safe to retry once", "No order ORD-4821; ask the customer to confirm the ID", or "Refund blocked: order is 112 days old (limit 90); do not retry, escalate".
