options.rationale: Correct. The docs recommend instructive error messages that say what went wrong and what Claude should try next. Flagging is_error and separating retryable from non-retryable cases lets Claude retry the timeout, ask for a corrected ID, and stop hammering the policy block.

options.text: Mark failures with is_error: true and pass through the raw exception class, HTTP status code, and stack trace (for example "TimeoutError: 504 at order_client.py:88" or "PolicyViolation: 403 refund_window") so Claude has full diagnostic detail to reason about the cause.
options.rationale: Anthropic's tool-writing guidance says error responses should communicate specific, actionable improvements rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks. A stack trace costs tokens and still leaves Claude guessing whether a retry can work.

options.text: When one of the parallel lookup_order calls fails, send its error in a separate user message after the message holding the successful results, so Claude handles the failure on its own turn.
options.rationale: Results for every tool_use block in a turn belong together in the next user message. Splitting them across separate user messages teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls, and it does nothing to make the error itself informative.

questions.explanation: Treat a tool error as a prompt: set is_error: true and write a short message that names the cause and the recovery step, including whether a retry can help. Generic strings, raw tracebacks, and blind retries all leave Claude guessing. Keep all results from a parallel batch together in one user message.
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractor a now also sets is_error (rationale updated: the generic message is still uninformative) and distractor c gained example raw error strings; key examples shortened while keeping is_error, cause plus next step, and the retry versus do-not-retry split.

questions.stem: A platform team is rolling out Claude Code to 40 engineers who share one monorepo. Every engineer should get the same two MCP servers when working in that repo: the company issue tracker (a remote HTTP server that authenticates with a per-person API token sent in an Authorization header) and a read-only metrics server. The team wants changes to these server definitions reviewed in pull requests like any other code, and no token may ever be committed. Separately, one engineer wants to trial an experimental stdio server in this repo without affecting her teammates. Which setup best meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Publish a wiki page of claude mcp add --scope user commands for both servers, with each engineer pasting in their own token, and have the experimenter add her server the same way.
options.rationale: User scope keeps tokens out of git, but the definitions live in each person's ~/.claude.json, so they are never reviewed in pull requests and will drift. User scope also loads the experimental server in all of her projects, not just this repo.

options.text: Commit a .mcp.json with both shared servers and a shared service-account token in the Authorization header so setup needs no per-person steps, and have the experimenter add her server to that file on a branch.
options.rationale: This commits a secret to version control and swaps per-person tokens for a shared credential, breaking two stated requirements.

options.text: Commit a .mcp.json with all three servers, relying on Claude Code's approval prompt for project-scoped servers so engineers who do not want the experimental server can decline it.
options.rationale: The approval prompt is a security check before project-scoped servers are used, not a way to keep one person's experiment out of the team's config. The experiment would still reach every teammate.

options.text: Commit a .mcp.json at the repo root with both shared servers, writing the header as "Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}" so each engineer supplies a token from their own environment, and have the experimenter add her server with the default local scope.
options.rationale: Correct. Project scope stores servers in a checked-in .mcp.json so the team shares one reviewed definition, environment variable expansion in headers keeps secrets out of git, and local scope keeps a personal server private to her and to this one project.

questions.explanation: Use project scope (a committed .mcp.json) for servers the whole team needs, with ${VAR} or ${VAR:-default} expansion for per-person secrets. Use local scope (the default) for personal or experimental servers in one project, and user scope for personal servers you want in every project. A same-named server in a higher-precedence scope (local, then project, then user) replaces the whole entry; fields are not merged.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent research system, a lead agent dispatches subagents to gather sources on narrow questions, such as supplier risk in a single region. Subagents reach the internal document store through an MCP server exposing two tools: list_documents, which returns all of roughly 4,000 documents with uuid, mime_type, size_bytes, created_at and title fields, and get_document(uuid). Traces show subagents spending most of their context window reading list_documents output and then calling get_document with UUIDs that do not exist. Which TWO changes to the tools are most likely to fix both problems? Select TWO.

options.text: Split get_document into get_document_text, get_document_sections and get_document_citations so each call returns a smaller payload.
options.rationale: This adds tools and round trips without touching the oversized listing or the invented IDs. Anthropic's guidance favors fewer, more capable tools because extra tools increase selection ambiguity.

options.text: Replace list_documents with search_documents(query, limit) that filters server-side, returns a small default page, and, when results are truncated, tells the agent how to narrow the query or fetch the next page.
options.rationale: Correct. A search tool with sensible defaults stops the agent from brute-force reading every row, and truncation messages steer it toward many small, targeted searches, which is the documented pattern for token efficiency.

options.text: Load the full 4,000-row listing into each subagent's system prompt and mark it for prompt caching so it is cheap to resend on every request.
options.rationale: Caching lowers cost and latency, but cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window (caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count), so the listing still crowds every subagent's context. It also does nothing about invented UUIDs.

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} for subagents so they must call a tool on every turn instead of answering from memory.
options.rationale: Forcing a tool call neither shrinks the listing nor makes identifiers easier to copy correctly, and some current models reject any and tool with a 400 error.

options.text: Return titles plus stable, human-readable identifiers such as slugs, drop low-signal fields like mime_type and size_bytes, and optionally offer a response_format parameter with concise and detailed options.
options.rationale: Correct. Anthropic reports that resolving opaque UUIDs to meaningful identifiers reduces hallucinations in retrieval, and returning only high-signal fields (with a concise mode) cuts tokens per result.

questions.explanation: Design tools around the agent's limited context: a filtered search with small defaults and helpful truncation messages beats returning everything. Return meaningful, stable identifiers and only the fields needed for the next step. Caching the bloat or forcing tool calls treats symptoms, not the tool design.
questions.verification_note: Option e is worded to fit both sources: the define-tools page calls slugs or UUIDs semantic, stable identifiers, while the writing-tools-for-agents article reports that resolving opaque UUIDs to meaningful language reduces hallucinations.

questions.stem: Your local stdio MCP server prints debug lines with print(). Claude Code starts it, but the connection fails with message parsing errors. What is the right fix?

options.text: Buffer the debug lines and flush them to stdout only after each response has been written.
options.rationale: Timing does not matter: the spec says the server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, so any stray text still corrupts the stream.

options.text: Raise MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS so the extra output fits within Claude Code's limit.
options.rationale: That variable sets Claude Code's token limit for MCP tool output (larger results are saved to a file instead). It has nothing to do with stray text breaking the JSON-RPC stream.

options.text: Send the debug lines to stderr and keep stdout for valid MCP messages only.
options.rationale: Correct. In the stdio transport the server may write logs to stderr, which the client can capture, forward, or ignore, while stdout must carry only MCP messages.

options.text: Switch the server to Streamable HTTP, since stdio servers cannot emit any logging.
options.rationale: stdio servers can log, just on stderr. Moving to HTTP adds a network service and its security concerns to fix a one-line logging mistake.

questions.explanation: With stdio, the client launches the server as a subprocess and stdout is the protocol channel: newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages and nothing else. Logs belong on stderr. Stray prints to stdout corrupt that channel.

questions.stem: On a model that supports forced tool use, you set tool_choice to {"type":"tool","name":"save_ticket"} and the prompt asks Claude to explain its reasoning first. What do you get back?

options.text: A save_ticket tool_use block with no explanation text before it.
options.rationale: Correct. With any or tool, the API prefills the assistant message to force a tool call, so Claude does not emit natural language before the tool_use block even when asked.

options.text: A short text explanation followed by the save_ticket tool_use block, since forcing only controls which tool is called.
options.rationale: Forcing does more than pick the tool: because the assistant turn is prefilled, no explanation text precedes the tool_use block.

options.text: A 400 error, because a forced tool_choice cannot be combined with a prompt that asks for text.
options.rationale: On models that support forced tool use the request succeeds and the request for an explanation is simply not honored. Some newer models reject any and tool with a 400 regardless of the prompt, but that is a model restriction, not a prompt conflict.

options.text: A plain text answer with no tool call, because explicit prompt instructions override tool_choice.
options.rationale: tool_choice is an API-level constraint that prompt text does not override. With type tool, Claude always calls the named tool.

questions.explanation: Forcing a tool (any or tool) prefills the assistant turn, so you get the tool_use block and no preamble. If you need reasoning plus a specific tool, use auto and name the tool in the user message. Check model support first: the docs list Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 as returning a 400 for any and tool, and recommend auto with strict tool use instead.
questions.verification_note: Drift: current docs say Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 return a 400 for tool_choice any or tool, while exam-era material treats forced tool use as available everywhere; the stem is scoped to models that support forced tool use so the key holds either way.

questions.stem: A telecom company's support agent runs on the Messages API with nine read tools that map one-to-one onto its REST endpoints (get_customer_by_id, get_customer_by_email, get_account, list_transactions, list_invoices, list_tickets, get_ticket, list_notes, get_plan) plus one action tool, issue_credit. Traces show three problems. Before its first reply the agent averages seven sequential tool calls, and median time to first reply is 19 seconds. list_transactions returns up to 500 raw rows full of internal codes, so long conversations run short of context. And the agent often calls get_account when it needed get_customer_by_id, because the two descriptions overlap. Which redesign best addresses all three problems?

options.text: Rewrite all nine read-tool descriptions to three or four sentences each, stating exactly what each returns and when to prefer it over its closest neighbor, and leave the endpoints and their responses unchanged.
options.rationale: Detailed descriptions are the biggest lever on tool selection and would cut the get_account mix-ups, but the agent still makes seven calls per reply and still reads up to 500 raw rows per transaction lookup.

options.text: Add the documented parallel tool use system prompt so the agent issues all seven lookups together in one turn instead of one after another, and keep the nine read tools and their response formats as they are.
options.rationale: Parallel calls cut round trips and so latency, but the same raw rows still land in context and the overlapping get_account and get_customer_by_id tools still invite the wrong pick.

options.text: Replace the read tools with one get_customer_context(email or ID) tool that gathers profile, plan, tickets, notes and recent transactions server-side and returns only fields support needs; keep issue_credit.
options.rationale: Correct. Anthropic recommends task-level tools that handle several API calls under the hood, and names get_customer_context as the replacement for get_customer_by_id, list_transactions and list_notes. One call replaces seven, high-signal fields cut context use, and removing overlapping tools removes the ambiguity.

options.text: Collapse the nine read tools into a single call_api tool with an endpoint enum listing all nine paths and a free-form params object, so the agent loads one compact tool definition instead of nine separate ones.
options.rationale: Grouping with an action parameter suits closely related operations, but this is still a thin wrapper over the endpoints: the agent makes the same seven calls, reads the same raw rows, and now picks the endpoint from an enum instead of a tool name.

questions.explanation: Tools that mirror API endpoints one-to-one push orchestration onto the agent: more round trips, raw payloads in context, and overlapping choices. Design tools around the task, letting one tool make several API calls and return only high-signal fields. Better descriptions or parallel calls each fix only one symptom.

questions.stem: An accounts-payable pipeline extracts invoice data by giving Claude one tool, record_invoice, whose input_schema has vendor_name, invoice_date, a required currency field, total, and a line_items array whose quantity is an integer. Requests set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"}. About 2% of calls fail downstream validation because quantity arrives as a string such as "2" or currency is missing, and a retry loop resubmits them. After the team moves the pipeline to Claude Opus 5.5, every request returns a 400 invalid_request_error saying tool_choice types tool and any are not supported for this model. The team wants schema-valid records and no retry loop. What should they change?

options.text: Use tool_choice auto, set strict: true on record_invoice with additionalProperties: false on each object, prompt Claude to record every invoice with it, and flag replies with no tool_use block.
options.rationale: Correct. The docs name auto plus strict tool use as the replacement on models that reject forced tool use. Strict mode constrains sampling to the schema, removing string-typed integers and missing required fields; prompting steers auto toward the tool, and the check catches a reply where Claude chose not to call it.

options.text: Change tool_choice to {"type": "any"}, which only requires that some tool is called rather than naming record_invoice, and keep the existing retry loop in place to catch the remaining 2% of malformed inputs.
options.rationale: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects any with the same 400 as tool, so every request still fails. It also keeps the retry loop the team wants to remove.

options.text: Use tool_choice auto without strict mode, expand every field description, add input_examples showing integer quantities and a three-letter currency code, and keep validating and retrying downstream.
options.rationale: Descriptions and input_examples help Claude format inputs, but strict tool use is what guarantees schema-valid tool inputs. Without it, string-typed integers and missing required fields can still occur, so the retry loop has to stay.

options.text: Pin the pipeline to the earlier model that still accepts forced tool_choice, and add a repair step that coerces string quantities to integers before the downstream validator checks each extracted record.
options.rationale: Pinning avoids the 400 for now but holds the pipeline on an older model, and a repair step cannot supply a missing required currency. Strict mode makes this kind of post-processing unnecessary.

questions.explanation: On models that reject forced tool_choice, use auto, ask for the tool in the prompt, and set strict: true so tool inputs are constrained to the schema. Strict mode removes type mismatches and missing required fields, so validate-and-retry loops can go. If you only need a JSON response rather than a tool call, structured outputs (output_config.format) is the other documented option.
questions.verification_note: Drift: exam-era guidance often recommends forcing the extraction tool with tool_choice; current docs say Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 return a 400 invalid_request_error for any and tool and recommend auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs, instead. The key is the documented replacement on those models.

questions.stem: A due-diligence research system has a lead agent that spawns subagents, each given the same tools from three MCP servers: the firm's internal deal-memo store, a licensed patent database, and public web search. The three search tools are named search, query and lookup, and each has a one-sentence description such as "Searches for documents." Traces show subagents running web searches for facts that exist only in internal deal memos, and querying the patent database for news coverage. Results from the wrong source flow back to the lead agent, which cites them as findings. Which change most directly fixes how subagents choose between these tools?

options.text: Have the lead agent decide the right source for each subtask and set the subagent's tool_choice to that search tool, so a subagent can never pick the wrong one.
options.rationale: The lead would choose from the same vague descriptions, the subagent loses the ability to switch sources as it learns, and Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 reject tool_choice tool with a 400.

options.text: Merge the three search tools into one search_all tool that sends each query to every backend at once and returns the combined results, so subagents never have to choose a source at all.
options.rationale: This avoids the choice by querying everything, which multiplies results and context use and leaves the subagent to sort relevant hits from noise. Anthropic advises returning only relevant, high-signal results.

options.text: Add several worked examples of correct tool picks to each subagent's system prompt, and keep the current tool names and one-sentence descriptions so none of the three MCP servers needs changes.
options.rationale: Examples can help, but the docs call detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance. Vague names and one-line descriptions keep misleading subagents on any question the examples do not cover.

options.text: Namespace names by service (dealmemos_search, patents_search, web_search) and rewrite each description to say what the source covers, what it returns, and when to use another tool instead.
options.rationale: Correct. The docs ask for descriptions that say when a tool should and should not be used, and for service namespacing so selection stays unambiguous as the library grows. Anthropic's research system found that bad descriptions send agents down wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose.

questions.explanation: Tool selection is driven mostly by names and descriptions. Namespace tools by service or resource, and write descriptions that cover scope, what comes back, and when a different tool is the right one. Forcing tool_choice, adding examples, or merging every source works around the ambiguity instead of removing it.
questions.verification_note: The writing-tools article notes that prefix versus suffix namespacing has non-trivial, model-dependent effects and should be chosen by evaluation; the key uses service prefixes, which define-tools gives as its example. The 400 for forced tool_choice in rationale a is a current-model detail; the key does not depend on it.

questions.stem: An internal developer assistant built on the Messages API has three client tools: read_file, write_file and run_tests. Claude often returns several tool_use blocks in one turn, such as write_file for two files followed by run_tests. The harness runs every batch with asyncio.gather and returns all results together in the next user message. Traces show two problems: run_tests sometimes starts before the writes finish and reports stale failures, and when a write_file call fails, run_tests still runs and Claude then chases misleading test errors. Batches of read_file calls work well in parallel, and the team wants to keep that speed. Which TWO changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Run batches containing write_file or run_tests sequentially in the listed order, stopping at the first failure, and keep running read_file-only batches concurrently.
options.rationale: Correct. The API does not prescribe an execution order. The docs suggest running tools with side effects or ordering requirements sequentially and independent reads in parallel, and call sequential execution that stops on the first failure valid.

options.text: Set disable_parallel_tool_use: true as a top-level request parameter so Claude never puts more than one tool call in a single turn and writes always finish before tests start.
options.rationale: The flag goes inside the tool_choice object, not at the top level of the request, and turning parallel calls off would also give up the fast read_file batches the team wants to keep.

options.text: Leave out the tool_use blocks the harness chose not to run and return results only for the calls that executed, so Claude is not distracted by calls that never ran.
options.rationale: The docs require one tool_result for every tool_use block, including calls you skip. Dropping them leaves Claude without any signal that run_tests never ran.

options.text: For each call skipped after a failure, return a tool_result with is_error: true and a short reason such as "Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed."
options.rationale: Correct. This is the documented pattern for a call you decide not to run. It keeps one result per tool_use and tells Claude why the tests did not run, so it fixes the failed write instead of chasing test output.

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true} so Claude makes exactly one tool call per turn and each write is confirmed before tests run.
options.rationale: With any, Claude must call a tool on every turn, so it can never finish with a plain text answer; it also gives up parallel reads, and Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 reject any with a 400.

questions.explanation: The API leaves execution order to you: run independent reads concurrently, and run calls with side effects or dependencies sequentially, stopping on failure. Every tool_use still gets a tool_result in the same user message, with is_error: true and a reason for anything skipped. You can also tell Claude in the system prompt to batch only independent calls; disabling parallel calls outright is a blunt fix that slows the safe batches too.
questions.verification_note: Rationales for b and e cite where disable_parallel_tool_use goes and the current 400 for tool_choice any on Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1; the key (a and d) does not depend on either, so the item is not marked volatile.

questions.stem: A tool's input_schema has a required field telling Claude to write out its full step-by-step reasoning for each call, and some requests now end in a reasoning_extraction refusal. What is the documented fix?

options.text: Make the field optional so Claude can skip it when needed, and retry any refused request on a fallback model.
options.rationale: The docs say this refusal category has no recommended fallback model and to change the prompt rather than retry. An optional field that still asks for full reasoning keeps the trigger in place.

options.text: Ask for a short explanation or the evidence behind the call, and read summarized thinking to see how Claude reasoned.
options.rationale: Correct. The docs say you can still ask for a short explanation or supporting evidence, and to see the reasoning by setting display to summarized and reading the thinking blocks.

options.text: Rename the field from reasoning to notes and keep the same instruction, since the field name is what triggers the refusal.
options.rationale: The trigger is what the field asks for, not its name: the docs say the wording can sit in a tool description, and they list the model's private notes and reasoning asked for in full as triggers too.

options.text: Set tool_choice to auto so Claude can skip the tool on calls where it would rather not share its reasoning.
options.rationale: tool_choice controls whether a tool is called, not what its input asks for. Every call that does use the tool still carries the reasoning request.

questions.explanation: Tool inputs, tool descriptions and system prompts that ask Claude to reproduce its reasoning can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal. Ask for a brief explanation or the evidence instead, and use summarized thinking when you need to see the reasoning. Change the prompt rather than retrying.
questions.verification_note: Drift: the reasoning_extraction refusal category and the define-tools advice to ask for an explanation rather than reasoning appear in current (October 2026) docs and are unlikely to be in exam-era material.

questions.stem: Your team is choosing how every tool should format the results it returns to Claude: JSON, XML or Markdown. What does Anthropic recommend in its guidance on writing tools for agents?

options.text: Return JSON from every tool, because strict: true can then validate each result against that tool's input_schema.
options.rationale: Strict tool use constrains the inputs Claude sends to your tool, not the results you return. A tool_result can carry a plain string or text, image and document blocks.

options.text: Return XML from every tool, since Claude is trained to attend to XML tags and they reliably beat JSON and Markdown.
options.rationale: Anthropic names XML, JSON and Markdown as structures that can each affect evaluation performance and says there is no one-size-fits-all solution, so XML is not a guaranteed winner.

options.text: Treat format as a design choice: the best structure varies by task and agent, so pick it using your own evaluations.
options.rationale: Correct. Anthropic says response structure can affect evaluation performance, that models tend to do better with formats that match their training data, that the best structure varies by task and agent, and to choose it based on your own evaluation.

options.text: Mirror each backend API's native response format, so Claude sees the same raw structure your engineers already work with.
options.rationale: Raw backend payloads carry low-signal fields. Anthropic advises returning only the high-signal information Claude needs and tuning response structure by evaluation, not inheriting it from the API.

questions.explanation: Tool response structure is a tunable part of tool design. Anthropic found that XML, JSON and Markdown can each change evaluation results, with no one-size-fits-all choice, so compare formats on your own evals and return only the fields Claude needs for its next step.
questions.verification_note: Replaces the drafted enum-capitalization item, which duplicated d4-012. Written and verified in the verify pass from the writing-tools article (response structure passage), with define-tools, handle-tool-calls and strict-tool-use backing the distractor rationales.

questions.stem: You changed list_threads to return thread titles and author names and dropped the thread IDs. Now the agent cannot call get_thread_replies, which needs a thread ID. What is the best fix?

options.text: Go back to returning raw records with every internal ID and field, since agents handle cryptic IDs as well as names.
options.rationale: Anthropic found agents work significantly better with natural-language names than cryptic identifiers, and returning every low-level field wastes context.

options.text: Add a get_thread_id(title) tool so the agent can resolve each title to its ID before calling get_thread_replies.
options.rationale: This adds a tool and an extra round trip per thread to recover data the first tool already had, and titles need not be unique, so a lookup can resolve to the wrong thread. More tools do not always mean better outcomes.

options.text: Have list_threads return the full reply text of every thread, so the agent never needs get_thread_replies.
options.rationale: This bloats every listing with content the agent may not need. Responses should carry only the fields Claude needs for its next step.

options.text: Return the ID next to the title and author, or add a response_format whose detailed mode includes it.
options.rationale: Correct. Anthropic's Slack example returns thread_ts and other IDs in a detailed response so the agent can make follow-up calls, while concise mode saves tokens. Agents may need both names and technical IDs.

questions.explanation: Drop low-signal technical fields, but keep the identifiers that downstream tools need. Anthropic's guidance pairs readable names for reasoning with IDs for chaining calls, for example by including IDs in a detailed response_format and leaving them out of a concise one.

questions.stem: A platform team is turning a prototype MCP server for the company's internal deployment API into a shared service. The prototype is a stdio server that each engineer runs locally from Claude Code, and it reads a long-lived personal API key from an environment variable. Security now requires central hosting so fixes ship once, sign-in through the company identity provider with per-user scopes, and no long-lived keys on laptops. In design review, one engineer proposes building on an in-house library that implements the 2024-11-05 HTTP+SSE transport, and having the server forward each caller's bearer token to the deployment API so that API can keep enforcing scopes. Which design best meets the requirements and the current MCP specification?

options.text: Host the server on the in-house HTTP+SSE library, since Claude Code can still connect to SSE endpoints, and forward each caller's bearer token to the deployment API so scopes are enforced in one place.
options.rationale: Both halves conflict with the spec. HTTP+SSE has been deprecated since protocol version 2025-03-26 and new implementations should not adopt it, and an MCP server must not pass through the token it received from the client.

options.text: Host it over Streamable HTTP as an OAuth resource server that publishes Protected Resource Metadata, accepts only tokens issued for its own URL, and uses a separate token to call the deployment API.
options.rationale: Correct. MCP servers must publish Protected Resource Metadata so clients can discover the authorization server, must reject tokens not issued for them, and must call upstream APIs with a separate token from the upstream authorization server. Claude Code runs the OAuth sign-in for remote servers through /mcp.

options.text: Keep the stdio server, but load the key from the operating system keychain instead of an environment variable and publish updates as an internal package so every laptop picks up fixes automatically.
options.rationale: The server still runs on every laptop with a long-lived key, and there is no identity-provider sign-in or per-user scope. The spec's OAuth flow is defined for HTTP transports; stdio servers are expected to take credentials from the environment.

options.text: Host the server over Streamable HTTP and have each engineer append a personal API key as a query parameter on the server URL, which keeps setup simple for clients that lack OAuth support.
options.rationale: The authorization spec says access tokens must not appear in the URI query string, where they leak into logs. It also keeps long-lived personal keys and skips identity-provider sign-in.

questions.explanation: A shared remote MCP server should use Streamable HTTP, which replaced the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport, and act as an OAuth resource server: advertise its authorization server through Protected Resource Metadata and accept only tokens whose audience is itself. When it calls an upstream API, it gets its own token for that API and never forwards the client's token, which avoids the confused deputy problem.
questions.verification_note: Current spec revision is 2026-07-28, which also removed protocol-level sessions and the GET stream from Streamable HTTP. The key does not depend on those changes: HTTP+SSE deprecation (since 2025-03-26), the Protected Resource Metadata requirement, audience validation, the ban on tokens in the URI query string and the no-passthrough rule appear in both the 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 revisions.

questions.stem: A product team uses Claude Code to generate GraphQL resolvers and client queries. Their checked-in CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,600 lines: build and test commands, a schema dump someone refreshes by hand every few months, a long guide to the team's resolver patterns, and instructions to curl the staging gateway with a shared service token pasted into the file. Developers report that Claude follows the build commands but writes queries against fields that were removed weeks ago, and security has flagged the committed token. The platform team already runs a remote MCP server for the gateway with schema introspection and query tools, and each user signs in to it with OAuth. How should the team restructure this setup to fix the stale queries and the committed token?

options.text: Move the schema dump, the pattern guide, and the curl instructions into a single skill so that content loads only when Claude works on GraphQL code, and leave the build commands in CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: On-demand loading cuts the per-request context cost, but the schema is still a hand-refreshed snapshot, so stale fields persist, and the shared token is still committed, now inside the skill.

options.text: Split CLAUDE.md into path-scoped files under .claude/rules/ that load when Claude opens GraphQL files, and change the curl instructions to read the shared token from an environment variable.
options.rationale: This gets the token out of the file, but the schema remains a static snapshot that drifts from the live gateway, and it rebuilds by hand a connection the existing MCP server already provides with per-user sign-in.

options.text: Add the gateway's MCP server to .mcp.json so each developer signs in with OAuth, turn the pattern guide into a skill, and cut CLAUDE.md down to build commands and short always-on rules.
options.rationale: Correct. MCP gives Claude live schema and query tools with connection and authentication handled by the server, a skill holds the pattern guide and loads only when used, and CLAUDE.md keeps only what every session needs. This is the documented Skill + MCP pattern.

options.text: Keep everything in CLAUDE.md and add a SessionStart hook that pulls a fresh schema from staging with the shared service token at the start of each session, so Claude always sees current fields.
options.rationale: The hook fixes staleness, but keeping everything in CLAUDE.md leaves the shared token committed, the 1,600-line file still loads on every request, and the full schema is added to context each session whether or not it is needed.

questions.explanation: Match each need to the feature built for it: MCP for live access to an external system, with auth handled by the server; a skill for reference material and workflows Claude needs only sometimes; CLAUDE.md for short rules every session needs. Live data pasted into always-on context goes stale and wastes context, and credentials never belong in instruction files.
questions.verification_note: Overlaps bank item d3-001 on CLAUDE.md size; this item's key turns on using the existing MCP server for live schema access with per-user OAuth instead of a pasted snapshot and a shared token, which is the documented Skill + MCP pattern.

questions.stem: A CI job runs claude -p with --permission-mode dontAsk on each pull request to link the PR to tracker issues and post a summary comment. The repository's committed .mcp.json defines a remote HTTP server named tracker whose Authorization header is "Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}". The CI secret store holds the token as TRACKER_API_KEY, and the job never exposes it under any other name. In the job log, claude mcp list shows a missing-variable warning for tracker, and the server rejects the connection with 401. In a debug run where an engineer set TRACKER_TOKEN by hand, the server connected, but Claude Code denied both of Claude's calls, to mcp__tracker__search_issues and mcp__tracker__add_comment. Which TWO changes are needed to make the job work? Select TWO.

options.text: Expose the stored secret to the claude step as TRACKER_TOKEN, since an unset variable with no default stays in the header as the literal text ${TRACKER_TOKEN}.
options.rationale: Correct. Expansion reads the variable named in .mcp.json. When it is unset and has no default, the config still loads, claude mcp list warns, and the unexpanded text is sent, which the server rejects.

options.text: Add enableAllProjectMcpServers: true to the committed .claude/settings.json, because claude -p skips .mcp.json servers that nobody has approved in an interactive session.
options.rationale: claude -p cannot show the approval prompt, so it connects project-scoped servers without asking. The debug run already connected, which shows approval was never the blocker.

options.text: Switch the run to --permission-mode acceptEdits, which approves tool calls automatically in non-interactive runs so the tracker tools no longer need their own rule.
options.rationale: acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands, not MCP tools, so the tracker calls would still be denied. The docs recommend allowedTools over permission modes for MCP access.

options.text: Pass --allowedTools "mcp__tracker__search_issues,mcp__tracker__add_comment" so the dontAsk run permits exactly those two tracker tools.
options.rationale: Correct. MCP tools need explicit permission, and dontAsk denies every call that would otherwise prompt unless an --allowedTools entry or allow rule covers it. MCP rules use the mcp__<server>__<tool> name.

options.text: Set MCP_TIMEOUT=60000 in the job so the remote server has enough time to finish its OAuth sign-in before the first turn starts, which avoids the 401 on a cold runner.
options.rationale: MCP_TIMEOUT sets how long Claude Code waits for a server to start. The server here authenticates with a bearer header, not an OAuth sign-in, and it answers 401 because the header still holds the unexpanded ${TRACKER_TOKEN} text.

questions.explanation: In CI, check two separate things for a project MCP server: that every ${VAR} in .mcp.json is actually set in the step's environment (an unset one stays as literal text), and that the run grants the MCP tools it needs by their mcp__<server>__<tool> names. claude -p connects .mcp.json servers without an approval prompt, but it still enforces tool permissions.
questions.verification_note: Drift: current docs say an unset ${VAR} with no default still loads, warns in claude mcp list, and is sent as literal text; earlier material may describe the config failing to load instead. Either way the fix is to set the variable. Current docs also say a claude -p session connects .mcp.json servers without an approval prompt, approved or not. The dontAsk mode and --allowedTools behavior rest on current CLI docs.

questions.stem: Your MCP server should offer a release-notes template that engineers pick explicitly and fill in with a version number, instead of Claude deciding when to use it. Which MCP primitive fits best?

options.text: A tool with a version parameter and a description telling Claude to call it only when asked.
options.rationale: Tools are model-controlled: Claude decides when to call them. A description asking for restraint is a request, not the user-selected workflow the stem describes.

options.text: A resource template such as notes://{version} that Claude Code reads into every session.
options.rationale: Resources are application-driven context identified by URIs. Claude Code attaches one when you @-mention it and gives Claude tools to read them, but it does not load them into every session, and a resource is data, not an invocable template.

options.text: A sampling request the server sends so the client's model drafts the release notes.
options.rationale: Sampling lets a server ask the client's model for a completion. It is not a primitive users browse and invoke.

options.text: A prompt with a version argument, which Claude Code shows to users as a slash command.
options.rationale: Correct. Prompts are user-controlled templates with optional arguments, typically exposed as slash commands, and Claude Code surfaces MCP prompts as commands.

questions.explanation: MCP splits server features by who controls them: prompts are user-controlled (slash commands), resources are application-driven (context the host attaches), and tools are model-controlled (Claude decides when to call). Pick the primitive by who should decide when it is used.

questions.stem: Your backend calls the Messages API with the MCP connector (mcp_servers) and wants Claude to use a vendor MCP server's tools, resources, and prompts. What does the connector give you?

options.text: Only its tools; resources and prompts are unsupported, and the server must be reachable over public HTTP.
options.rationale: Correct. The connector supports only MCP tool calls, and the server must be publicly exposed over Streamable HTTP or SSE.

options.text: Tools and resources, with each of the server's prompts merged into the system prompt at the start of every request.
options.rationale: The connector does not support resources or prompts at all, and it never injects prompts into the system prompt.

options.text: All three primitives, as long as the server runs locally over stdio on the same host as your backend process.
options.rationale: Local stdio servers cannot be connected directly. The connector needs an https URL to a publicly exposed server, and it still offers only tools.

options.text: All three primitives, once the API has run the vendor server's OAuth sign-in flow for you on the first request.
options.rationale: The API does not run the OAuth flow. Your application obtains and refreshes the token and passes it as authorization_token, and only tools are supported.

questions.explanation: The Messages API MCP connector lets Claude call tools on remote MCP servers without you writing an MCP client, but only tools: no resources, no prompts, no local stdio servers. You supply the OAuth token yourself; for anything beyond that, run your own MCP client.
questions.verification_note: Drift: the connector is a beta behind the mcp-client-2025-11-20 header (a later mcp-client-2026-09-15 header adds tool-list pinning); the earlier mcp-client-2025-04-04 version is deprecated and put tool settings on the server entry instead of an mcp_toolset in tools. The tools-only, remote-only (https URL, Streamable HTTP or SSE) limitations apply to the current version.

questions.stem: Your MCP server's get_schema tool returns about 150,000 characters of text, and Claude Code saves each result to a file. What server-side change keeps the full result inline, with no setup by users?

options.text: Document that each user should export MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=60000 before starting Claude Code.
options.rationale: Raising the variable can lift the token limit for tools that declare none, but it is a per-user environment change, which the stem rules out. The annotation lets the server raise this one tool's threshold with no user setup.

options.text: Set _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] to 200000 on get_schema in tools/list.
options.rationale: Correct. Claude Code raises that tool's persist-to-disk threshold to the annotated value, up to 500,000 characters, and for text the annotation applies independently of MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS, so users don't need to raise the variable.

options.text: Return the schema as a PNG image of the tables so it skips the text size limits.
options.rationale: Image results stay subject to MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS and the annotation does not apply to them. A picture of a schema is also harder for Claude to use than text.

options.text: Mark the server alwaysLoad: true so its tool results are exempt from deferral.
options.rationale: alwaysLoad is a field on the server's entry in Claude Code's MCP config that exempts its tool schemas from tool search deferral at startup. It has no effect on how large tool results are handled.

questions.explanation: Claude Code warns when MCP output passes 10,000 tokens and saves a result with no image content that exceeds MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS (25,000 tokens by default) to a file Claude reads when needed. A server author can raise one tool's text threshold with _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"], up to 500,000 characters, so users change nothing; for servers that do not declare it, users can raise MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS instead.
questions.verification_note: Drift: the anthropic/maxResultSizeChars annotation (500,000-character ceiling) is recent and may postdate exam-era material, which may mention only MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS and its 25,000-token default. Rewritten so the key does not rest on a 50,000-character default threshold: current docs state the token limit and the annotation but give no character figure for the default persist-to-disk threshold, so the stem now rules out per-user setup instead.

questions.stem: Your team's monorepo has a single root CLAUDE.md, committed to git, that has grown to about 700 lines. It holds repo-wide build and test commands, detailed rules that only matter inside the payments/ service, React conventions that only apply under web/, a 30-step release procedure the team runs about twice a month, and one engineer's personal sandbox URLs. Everyone launches Claude Code from the repo root. Engineers report that Claude increasingly ignores rules it used to follow, and teammates are confused by the sandbox URLs showing up in their sessions. You want better adherence without throwing away any of the guidance. Which restructuring is the best fit?

options.text: Split the content into topic files (payments.md, web.md, release.md, sandbox.md) and pull each one back into the root CLAUDE.md with @path imports, so the root file stays under the documented 200-line target and each topic is reviewed on its own.
options.rationale: Imports help organize a long file but do not reduce its context cost, because imported files are expanded and loaded at launch, so a short root file still loads all 700 lines. The personal URLs would also still reach every teammate.

options.text: Delete the project CLAUDE.md and have each engineer copy the content into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, pruning whatever they personally do not need.
options.rationale: User-level CLAUDE.md is personal and loads in every project on that machine, so shared standards stop being version-controlled and drift per engineer. Whatever each person keeps still loads every session.

options.text: Keep only repo-wide facts in the root CLAUDE.md, move the payments/ and web/ rules into path-scoped .claude/rules/ files or nested CLAUDE.md files, turn the release procedure into a skill, and put the sandbox URLs in a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md.
options.rationale: Correct. Path-scoped rules and subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load only when Claude works with matching files, a skill's body loads only when used, and CLAUDE.local.md holds personal project notes outside source control, so the always-loaded file shrinks without losing guidance.

options.text: Move the entire file to the managed policy CLAUDE.md location via MDM, so the instructions cannot be excluded and carry more weight than project-level files.
options.rationale: Managed CLAUDE.md applies to every session on the machine in every repository, which is the wrong scope for repo-specific rules. It is still loaded as context, not enforced, so it does not raise adherence or shrink what loads.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md content loads every session and long files reduce adherence, so keep the always-loaded file short (the docs target under 200 lines) and push part-of-the-codebase rules into path-scoped rules or nested CLAUDE.md files, multi-step procedures into skills, and personal notes into CLAUDE.local.md. @imports organize content but do not lower its context cost.
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractor a now cites the 200-line target the root file would meet (rationale updated: imports still load everything at launch); key punctuation and wording tightened with all four moves kept.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Claude Code nightly in CI to fix lint failures in a service repository and open a pull request. Today the job runs `claude -p "fix all lint errors"` with default settings, and the repo's CLAUDE.md says "Never modify files in db/migrations/." Last week Claude reformatted a migration file after a lint message suggested it, and a downstream script that posts the run summary and cost to Slack broke because it scrapes plain text. The new requirements: Claude may edit source files and run only the project's lint and git commands, with anything else refused automatically instead of waiting for approval; Claude's file edits under db/migrations/ must be blocked regardless of what Claude decides; and the summary and cost must come from machine-readable output. Which configuration best meets all three requirements?

options.text: Run with `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` so the job never stalls, change the CLAUDE.md line to start with "IMPORTANT:", and add `--output-format json`.
options.rationale: bypassPermissions runs everything without checks and is meant for isolated containers and VMs, so nothing limits Claude to lint and git commands. CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, so added emphasis still cannot block an edit.

options.text: Run with `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, add a PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write that exits 2 when the path is under db/migrations/, and use `--output-format stream-json --verbose`, reading the final result message.
options.rationale: PostToolUse fires after the tool call succeeds, and exit 2 there only shows stderr to Claude because the tool already ran, so the migration edit has already happened. The streaming output would work; the guard does not.

options.text: Run with `--permission-mode plan` so no unreviewed edits can happen, keep the CLAUDE.md line as a backup, and add `--output-format json`.
options.rationale: Plan mode keeps its edit block in non-interactive -p runs, so Claude could only propose a plan and would fix no lint errors at all. It overshoots the requirement instead of scoping it.

options.text: Run with `--permission-mode dontAsk` and `--allowedTools` listing Edit plus the lint and git Bash commands, add `Edit(/db/migrations/**)` to `permissions.deny` in .claude/settings.json, and add `--output-format json`, reading `result` and `total_cost_usd`.
options.rationale: Correct. dontAsk denies every call that would otherwise prompt while still running pre-approved tools, deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and apply to all built-in file-editing tools, and the JSON payload includes the result text and a cost estimate.

questions.explanation: In unattended runs, put constraints in enforced configuration rather than instructions: dontAsk plus an explicit allowlist makes the run fail closed, and a deny rule (or a PreToolUse hook) blocks forbidden edits no matter what Claude decides. PostToolUse cannot prevent an action because it runs after the tool succeeds, and --output-format json gives scripts parseable result and cost fields.

questions.stem: Your developer-experience team ships a project skill at .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md. Two problems have surfaced. First, Claude almost never picks the skill up on its own when engineers say things like "draft the changelog for v4.2." Second, when someone does invoke it, the 900-line SKILL.md (which embeds the full 700-line editorial style guide) floods the conversation. The current frontmatter is only `description: Release notes helper`. Which changes most directly fix these two problems? Select TWO.

options.text: Rewrite `description` (optionally adding `when_to_use`) to lead with what the skill does and the phrases engineers actually use, such as "release notes", "changelog", and version numbers.
options.rationale: Correct. Claude uses the description to decide when to apply a skill, so a vague one-liner rarely matches; the docs say to put the key use case first and include trigger phrases.

options.text: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` so Claude Code loads the skill eagerly instead of waiting for a description match.
options.rationale: This does the opposite: it prevents Claude from loading the skill automatically and removes its description from context, leaving only manual /release-notes invocation.

options.text: Paste the style guide into the project CLAUDE.md so it is always available and the skill body can shrink.
options.rationale: CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so this moves 700 lines into every conversation, including ones that have nothing to do with release notes. It makes the context problem worse overall.

options.text: Move the style guide into a supporting file such as style-guide.md in the skill directory, link it from SKILL.md, and keep SKILL.md to the core workflow.
options.rationale: Correct. Supporting files keep SKILL.md focused while letting Claude read detailed reference material only when needed; the docs suggest keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines.

options.text: Put the full style guide text in the `description` field so Claude can match requests against its vocabulary.
options.rationale: Descriptions sit in context for every session so Claude knows what is available, and the combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing, so this wastes context and most of it would be cut.

questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: only the short description is in context up front, the SKILL.md body loads when the skill is invoked, and supporting files load only when Claude needs them. Fix discovery by writing a specific, trigger-rich description, and fix bloat by moving bulky reference material into linked supporting files.
questions.verification_note: Keys confirmed against the skills page frontmatter reference, its supporting-files guidance, and its tip to keep SKILL.md under 500 lines. Drift: the 1,536-character listing cap cited in option e's rationale dates from Claude Code v2.1.105 (2026-04-13), after a 250-character cap added in v2.1.86 (2026-03-27); the keyed answers do not depend on either number.

questions.stem: Before a multi-file auth refactor in code you don't know well, you want Claude to explore and propose an approach, with edits blocked until you approve. How should you start?

options.text: Start with `claude --permission-mode acceptEdits` and ask Claude to plan first.
options.rationale: acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands, so nothing blocks Claude from editing before you approve anything.

options.text: Start with `claude --permission-mode plan` (or press Shift+Tab until plan mode is on).
options.rationale: Correct. Plan mode has Claude read files, explore, and write a plan without editing source; edits stay blocked until you approve the plan.

options.text: Add "Do not edit files until I approve a plan" to the project CLAUDE.md.
options.rationale: CLAUDE.md is context Claude tries to follow, not enforced configuration, so it shapes behavior but does not actually block edits.

options.text: Start with `claude --permission-mode dontAsk` so Claude works without prompts and saves its proposed plan for your review before editing.
options.rationale: dontAsk is built for locked-down CI and scripts: it silently denies anything that would prompt and has no plan review or approval step, so nothing hands a plan to you before implementation.

questions.explanation: Plan mode separates exploration from execution: Claude researches and proposes, and edits stay blocked until you approve the plan. The docs recommend it when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or the code is unfamiliar, and suggest skipping it when you could describe the diff in one sentence.

questions.stem: Project settings deny `Bash(git push *)`. A PreToolUse hook in settings returns permissionDecision "allow" for `git push origin main`. What does Claude Code do?

options.text: Blocks the push, because deny rules are evaluated regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returns.
options.rationale: Correct. A hook that returns "allow" does not bypass deny rules from the permission system; a matching deny rule still blocks the call.

options.text: Runs the push, because PreToolUse hooks run before permission rules and the first decision wins.
options.rationale: Only a blocking hook (exit 2 or a "deny" decision) short-circuits before rules are evaluated. An allow decision does not skip deny or ask rules.

options.text: Runs the push, because a hook's "allow" overrides project-level rules and only deny rules in managed settings still hold over a hook.
options.rationale: Deny rules from every settings scope, not only managed settings, are evaluated regardless of a hook's "allow", so the project deny rule blocks the push.

options.text: Runs the push, because the hook's decision about one exact command is more specific than the rule's wildcard pattern.
options.rationale: Specificity does not change evaluation order. Rules are checked deny, then ask, then allow, and an allow cannot carve an exception out of a deny.

questions.explanation: Deny rules are the hard floor: they are evaluated before allow rules from any scope and are not bypassed by a PreToolUse hook's "allow". Hooks can tighten permissions (an exit 2 blocks even an allowed call) but cannot loosen a deny.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed for hooks defined in settings files and plugin hooks.json. The permissions page notes that an installed mod handling tool.check can override deny rules on machines without managed settings or a Team/Enterprise sign-in; the stem specifies a settings hook to stay within the confirmed case. Drift: Claude Code v2.1.77 (2026-03-16) fixed a bug where a PreToolUse "allow" could bypass deny rules, and earlier hooks docs said "allow" bypasses the permission system, so exam-era material written before that fix may expect the push to run.

questions.stem: A developer's repo commits .claude/settings.json with an ask rule `Bash(git push *)` and deny rules `Read(./.env)` and `Read(./.env.*)`. She accepted the workspace trust dialog on first launch. In her own untracked .claude/settings.local.json she sets `model` to a different model, and that override works. She also chose "Yes, and don't ask again" on a push prompt, which saved `Bash(git push *)` as an allow rule in her local file, and she added `Read(./.env.local)` as an allow rule there so Claude can debug her local config. Claude still prompts before every push and still refuses to read .env.local. She argues that project local settings outrank shared project settings, so her rules should win. What explains the behavior?

options.text: For permission keys the shared file outranks the local one, because Claude Code ranks team files above personal overrides when a setting is security-sensitive.
options.rationale: There is no such reversal: project local settings still sit above shared project settings. The outcome comes from list merging plus the deny, ask, allow evaluation order, which would block her allow rules even if every rule lived in one file.

options.text: Permission lists from every file are combined, and each call is checked against deny, then ask, then allow, so the shared ask and deny rules match before her allow rules.
options.rationale: Correct. List keys such as permissions.allow merge across files instead of overriding, and the first match in deny, ask, allow order decides, so a local allow cannot outrank a shared ask or deny. Scope precedence only picks the winner for single-valued keys such as model.

options.text: Her allow rules match at the same specificity as the shared rules; narrower patterns such as `Bash(git push origin feature/*)` would take precedence over the shared ones.
options.rationale: Rule specificity does not change the evaluation order. A matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches, and an allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule.

options.text: Her rules belong on the command line: `--allowedTools` sits above both project files in the precedence order, so allow rules passed there override the shared ask and deny rules.
options.rationale: The command line outranks project files for single-valued keys, but a tool denied at any level cannot be allowed by another level, and allow rules from any source are only reached after deny and ask rules fail to match.

questions.explanation: Settings precedence (managed, command line, local, shared project, user) picks the winner for single-valued keys, but permission rules from every scope are pooled and evaluated deny, then ask, then allow. A personal allow rule can never loosen a shared ask or deny; to relax one, change the shared rule itself.
questions.verification_note: The key rests on the deny, ask, allow evaluation order and list merging, both stated on the permissions and settings pages; the settings troubleshooting section describes this exact case, where a "Yes, and don't ask again" allow saved to the local file still prompts because of a project ask rule. The stem states the folder is trusted and the local file is untracked, so the permissions page's workspace-trust holds on local allow rules don't apply.

questions.stem: Your team wants a migration reviewer that Claude hands work to after anyone edits files under db/migrations/. It must never edit files or run shell commands, it should run on Haiku to keep cost down, the files it reads should stay out of the main conversation, and every engineer should get it from the repo. An engineer drafted it as .claude/skills/migration-review/SKILL.md with `allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob` and `model: haiku`, assuming allowed-tools limits what Claude can call. In a session running in acceptEdits mode, Claude edited a migration while following the skill, and the review pasted several full migration files into the main conversation. Which change best meets all four requirements?

options.text: Keep the skill and add `context: fork`, so it runs in an isolated subagent whose tool set is exactly the list in the skill's allowed-tools field.
options.rationale: allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the invoking turn but never restricts which tools are available. With context: fork and no agent field, the skill runs in the general-purpose subagent, which gets every tool available to subagents.

options.text: Define it in ~/.claude/agents/migration-reviewer.md with `tools: Read, Grep, Glob` and `model: haiku`, since user subagents take priority over project subagents.
options.rationale: A file in ~/.claude/agents/ is personal, so teammates never get it from the repo, and user subagents have lower priority than project subagents in .claude/agents/, not higher.

options.text: Commit .claude/agents/migration-reviewer.md with a description saying when to delegate, `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`, and `model: haiku`.
options.rationale: Correct. A project subagent committed to .claude/agents/ reaches the whole team, its tools allowlist leaves out Edit, Write, and Bash, model: haiku routes it to the cheaper model, and it works in its own context and returns only a summary.

options.text: Keep the skill and replace allowed-tools with `disallowed-tools: Edit Write Bash`, so those tools are removed from Claude's pool while the skill is active.
options.rationale: disallowed-tools removes those tools only while the skill is active, and the restriction clears at the next user message. The skill also still runs inline, so the migration files it reads still land in the main conversation.

questions.explanation: A skill adds instructions to the current conversation; a subagent gives a task its own context window, tool allowlist, and model. When a helper must be unable to edit, run cheaply, and keep its reads out of the main thread, define a project subagent with tools and model in its frontmatter, and don't rely on a skill's allowed-tools, which pre-approves tools but never restricts them.
questions.verification_note: Confirmed on the sub-agents page (scope priority table with project above user, tools allowlist example, model aliases including haiku, work done in its own context with only the summary returned, background subagents still keep Edit, Write, and Bash) and the skills page (allowed-tools "does not restrict which tools are available", the grant and disallowed-tools clear at the next message, context: fork defaults to general-purpose). The keyed subagent answer rests on long-standing subagent frontmatter. Volatile only because distractors a and d rest on current skill frontmatter semantics; no official page was found that describes allowed-tools as restrictive, so no Drift claim is made.

questions.stem: Your developer-experience team keeps a template repo whose .claude/ folder holds three skills (one named changelog), a security-reviewer subagent, a PostToolUse formatting hook in .claude/settings.json, and a .mcp.json for the internal ticket server. Forty service repos copy this folder by hand and drift apart. The team wants one versioned package that repos install and update. Their first plugin attempt puts plugin.json, skills/, agents/, and hooks/hooks.json all inside dx-kit/.claude-plugin/. With `claude --plugin-dir ./dx-kit` the plugin appears in /plugin, but none of its skills or agents load. Several service repos also define their own changelog skill. Which plan is correct?

options.text: Keep syncing the template's .claude/ folder into each repo with a scheduled script, since a plugin can package skills but not subagents, hooks, or MCP servers.
options.rationale: A plugin packages skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers as one unit, and a marketplace gives every repo the same versioned set with updates, which a copy script does not.

options.text: Fix the layout, then have each service repo rename its own changelog skill first, because an enabled plugin's changelog skill replaces the project's /changelog.
options.rationale: Plugin skills are namespaced, so dx-kit's skill loads as /dx-kit:changelog while a repo's own changelog skill keeps /changelog. Both stay available, so no rename is needed.

options.text: Fix the layout but keep the hook in each repo's .claude/settings.json, since a plugin's hooks/hooks.json only runs in repos that define no hooks of their own.
options.rationale: Plugin hooks merge with user and project hooks instead of yielding to them, and hooks carry no plugin prefix, so a hook kept in both settings.json and hooks/hooks.json runs twice each time its event fires.

options.text: Keep only plugin.json in .claude-plugin/, move skills/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, and .mcp.json to the dx-kit/ root, and list it in an internal marketplace.
options.rationale: Correct. Only plugin.json belongs inside .claude-plugin/, and components saved there don't load. Components go at the plugin root, and a marketplace lets repos install the plugin by name and receive updates.

questions.explanation: A plugin is the unit for sharing a set of skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers across many repos with versioned updates. Keep only the manifest in .claude-plugin/, put components at the plugin root, and rely on the plugin-name prefix to keep skills and agents from colliding; hooks carry no prefix, so remove the originals from settings after migrating.
questions.verification_note: The plugins create page has the layout warning ("Only plugin.json goes inside .claude-plugin/. Components saved there don't load."), the missing-skills troubleshooting entry, marketplace install-by-name with updates, and the migration note that hooks have no prefix so a hook in both a settings file and hooks/hooks.json runs twice. The hooks page says a plugin's hooks merge with user and project hooks, and that identical handlers dedupe only across settings files while a plugin's copy stays separate, which agrees with the create page. The skills page says a plugin skill and a same-named project skill both load. Option c was rewritten to rest on hook merging rather than the dedupe detail, and the skill was renamed from review to changelog because /review is an alias of the bundled /code-review skill, which would muddy option b.

questions.stem: You are reviewing a pull request that adds permission rules to a project's shared .claude/settings.json. Every teammate has already trusted the repo, and the project's .mcp.json defines a server named github. Each rule is listed with the intent its author wrote next to it. Which TWO rules behave as their authors intend? Select TWO.

options.text: Allow `Bash(npm run test *)`: run the test script without a prompt, both bare and with extra arguments such as `-- --watch`.
options.rationale: Correct. A trailing ` *` matches any following text and, as the rule's only wildcard, also matches the bare command, so this covers `npm run test` and `npm run test -- --watch`.

options.text: Deny `Read(/etc/ssl/private/**)`: block reads of the machine's absolute /etc/ssl/private directory on every developer laptop.
options.rationale: A single leading slash anchors at the settings source, which for project settings is the primary working directory, so this blocks <project>/etc/ssl/private. An absolute path needs `//etc/ssl/private/**`.

options.text: Allow `Bash(git * main)`: let Claude run read-only git commands against main, such as `git log main` and `git diff main`, without asking.
options.rationale: The `*` stands in for the subcommand, so this matches every git subcommand that ends in main, including `git push origin main`. Claude Code warns at startup about an allow rule with a `*` before the subcommand.

options.text: Deny `WebFetch(domain:*.example.com)`: block fetches to example.com itself and to every one of its subdomains at any depth.
options.rationale: A leading `*.` matches subdomains at any depth but not example.com itself, so fetches to the bare domain are not blocked. A second rule for `domain:example.com` is needed.

options.text: Allow `mcp__github__get_*`: auto-approve only the github MCP server's tools whose names begin with get_.
options.rationale: Correct. Allow rules accept a tool-name glob after a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix, so this auto-approves the github server's tools whose names start with get_ and nothing else.

questions.explanation: Permission specifiers are literal: a `*` in a Bash rule stands in for whatever text sits in its place, including the subcommand, a single leading slash in a Read or Edit path anchors at the settings source rather than the filesystem root, and a `*.` domain wildcard leaves out the apex domain. Read each rule the way Claude Code matches it, not the way its comment hopes.
questions.verification_note: All five behaviors are stated on the permissions page (wildcard table and the rule that a trailing ` *` that is the only wildcard also matches the bare command, /path anchoring table, git * main row and startup warning, WebFetch domain wildcards, allow globs only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix). Stem now says the repo is trusted, since project allow rules wait for workspace trust. Relevance is current because the key rests on fine-grained matching rules (bare-command match for a trailing ` *`, MCP tool-name globs in allow rules). Drift: WebFetch wildcards require Claude Code v2.1.172 or later to match fetches; on older versions option d still fails its intent because the rule blocks nothing.

questions.stem: You start Claude Code in packages/web/ of a monorepo. CLAUDE.md files exist at the repo root, in packages/web/, and in packages/web/legacy/. Which of them are in context at launch?

options.text: The root and packages/web/ files; packages/web/legacy/CLAUDE.md joins once Claude reads files there.
options.rationale: Correct. CLAUDE.md files in the working directory and every directory above it load at launch, concatenated from the root down, while files in subdirectories below load on demand when Claude reads files in them.

options.text: Only packages/web/CLAUDE.md, because the file nearest the working directory overrides those above it.
options.rationale: Discovered CLAUDE.md files are concatenated, not overridden. The nearer file is simply read later, so the root file still loads.

options.text: All three, because Claude Code reads every CLAUDE.md under the repository root when the session starts.
options.rationale: Only the working directory and its ancestors load at launch. A CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory below the working directory waits until Claude reads files there.

options.text: Only the root CLAUDE.md, because project instructions always load from the git repository root.
options.rationale: Loading walks up from the working directory, so packages/web/CLAUDE.md loads as well; the repository root is not the only source.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md files from the launch directory and its ancestors load at startup and are concatenated from the filesystem root down, so instructions nearer the launch directory are read last. Files in deeper subdirectories load lazily when Claude reads files there, which keeps area-specific guidance out of context until it's needed.
questions.verification_note: Memory page: CLAUDE.md files above the working directory load at launch, files in subdirectories load on demand when Claude reads files there, and all discovered files are concatenated from the filesystem root down. The large-codebases start-location table agrees ("That directory's plus every ancestor's").

questions.stem: A file .claude/rules/api.md starts with frontmatter `paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]`. When does Claude Code add this rule to Claude's context?

options.text: At launch in every session, like any file in .claude/rules/; the paths list only tells Claude which files the rule covers.
options.rationale: Only rules without a paths field load at launch. A rule with paths is conditional and loads when Claude works with matching files.

options.text: When a prompt mentions the API, because Claude matches each rule's paths and content against the request like a skill description.
options.rationale: Rules are not matched against the prompt the way skill descriptions are. A path-scoped rule loads based on the files Claude works with.

options.text: Whenever any tool call names a matching path, including Bash commands such as grep or sed that Claude runs against src/api/.
options.rationale: Matching is tied to the Read, Write, and Edit tools, not to every tool call that mentions a path, so a Bash grep or sed over src/api/ does not load the rule.

options.text: When Claude uses Read, Write, or Edit on a matching file; other tool use, such as a Bash grep over src/api/, doesn't load it.
options.rationale: Correct. Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude uses the Read, Write, or Edit tool on a file matching the pattern, not on every tool use.

questions.explanation: A .claude/rules/ file without paths loads every session with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md, while one with paths loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file. If Claude explores only through Bash, path-scoped guidance may not be in context yet, so put rules that must hold from the first turn in an unconditional file.
questions.verification_note: The memory page states verbatim: "Path-scoped rules trigger when Claude uses the Read, Write, or Edit tool on a file matching the pattern, not on every tool use," and rules without paths "are loaded at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md." Relevance is current and the item volatile because the key rests on that exact trigger list, a fine-grained detail, and the page records recent fixes to path-scoped rules (v2.1.207 invalid patterns, v2.1.211 --setting-sources, v2.1.217 brace expansion). No change to the trigger itself was found, so no Drift claim is made.

questions.stem: Your repo has .claude/commands/deploy.md. A teammate adds .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md with different steps. When someone types /deploy, what runs?

options.text: The skill, because a skill takes precedence over a .claude/commands/ file that has the same name.
options.rationale: Correct. When a skill and a file in .claude/commands/ share a name, /deploy runs the skill.

options.text: The command file, because the older .claude/commands/ format keeps its name when a newer skill reuses it.
options.rationale: Command files are the older format and still work, but on a name clash the skill takes precedence over the command file.

options.text: Both, one after the other, since Claude Code merges a command and a skill of the same name into one prompt.
options.rationale: Claude Code resolves a name clash to a single entry. It does not merge or chain a command and a skill that share a name.

options.text: Whichever one Claude judges a better match for the request, since both register /deploy and Claude picks by description.
options.rationale: Typing /deploy at the start of a message runs the resolved entry directly. Claude does not choose between same-named entries by description.

questions.explanation: Custom commands have been merged into skills: .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy, and on a clash the skill wins. Prefer skills for new work, since they add supporting files and control over who invokes them, and retire the old command file so the team isn't surprised.
