The key comes from the best-practices line that multishot examples work with thinking and should be presented as problem, method and expected answer.

questions.stem: On a current Claude model with adaptive thinking, your agent thinks at length on routine steps and latency suffers. What does Anthropic recommend adjusting first?

options.text: Add "Do not think; answer immediately" to the system prompt so that every request skips thinking.
options.rationale: Prompt-based steering works but is wording-sensitive and can lower quality on steps that need reasoning. Anthropic suggests it only if triggering is still wrong after you set effort.

options.text: Lower the effort level, which is the calibrated control for how readily and deeply Claude thinks.
options.rationale: Correct. Effort is the primary lever for thinking, and Anthropic advises lowering it before reaching for prompt-based steering because it is a calibrated control rather than a wording-sensitive instruction.

options.text: Set thinking.budget_tokens to a small value such as 1024 to cap the reasoning on each request.
options.rationale: budget_tokens is the legacy manual extended-thinking control: deprecated on Claude 4.6 models and rejected with a 400 error on Claude 4.7 and later. Use effort, with max_tokens as the hard cap.

options.text: Reduce max_tokens so the thinking runs out of room sooner and the model is pushed to answer.
options.rationale: max_tokens caps thinking and response together, so cutting it tends to truncate replies with stop_reason max_tokens rather than make the model think less.

questions.explanation: With adaptive thinking, Claude decides per request whether and how much to think, and effort sets that posture. Lower effort first, add system prompt or per-message steering only if triggering still does not fit, and measure quality either way.
questions.verification_note: Steering thinking page: "If you want Claude to think less often, lower the effort level before reaching for prompt-based steering"; prompt steering is wording-sensitive and may reduce quality. Drift: budget_tokens is deprecated on Claude 4.6 models and returns a 400 error on Claude 4.7 and later, with effort replacing it; exam-era material may still present budget_tokens as the main way to bound thinking. Effort level names and defaults vary by model (medium is the default on Claude Opus 5.5, high elsewhere).

questions.stem: Your team runs a due-diligence research agent on the Messages API. A single agent plans the work, then runs every web search and page fetch itself; each fetched page adds 8,000 to 15,000 tokens of raw text to the conversation. A typical question splits into five or six largely independent subquestions (financials, litigation, leadership, and so on). On long runs, after roughly 40 fetches, quality drops: the agent re-fetches pages it already read, mixes up which source said what, and the final report misattributes facts. The report must cite a source URL for every claim, including facts found early in the run. Which change best addresses the degradation?

options.text: Raise max_tokens to the model's maximum so the agent has more room to hold everything it has read across the run.
options.rationale: max_tokens sets the output limit for a response; it adds no room for input, and stuffing more into context does not help because recall degrades as token count grows.

options.text: Enable tool result clearing with keep set to 3 and make no other changes, so old page text is removed automatically once the context passes a threshold and the agent keeps working from its recent fetches.
options.rationale: Clearing shrinks the context, but each cleared result is replaced with placeholder text; with nothing persisting the findings (no notes or memory tool), the early page content behind the facts the report must cite and attribute is gone from context.

options.text: Have the lead agent delegate each subquestion to a subagent that searches and fetches in its own context window and returns a condensed summary with the source URL for each fact.
options.rationale: Correct. Subagents explore in clean context windows and return condensed, distilled summaries (often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens), so the lead agent coordinates over attributed findings instead of hundreds of thousands of tokens of raw page text.

options.text: Append all fetched page text to the system prompt behind a cache_control breakpoint so resending it on every turn is cheaper and faster, and every early source stays available for citation.
options.rationale: Caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix, but cached tokens still count toward the context window, so keeping every page in context leaves context rot untouched; and changing the system prompt after every fetch invalidates the system and messages caches anyway.

questions.explanation: Context rot means recall degrades as the context grows, so the fix is less raw text in the coordinating context, not more room or cheaper tokens. Subagents isolate heavy exploration and hand back distilled, attributed summaries. If you clear old tool results instead, persist what matters first (structured notes or the memory tool).
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractors b and d lengthened with still-wrong detail (working from recent fetches; every early source kept in context for citation) and d's rationale updated; key tightened with per-subagent context windows, condensed summaries, and per-fact source URLs kept.

questions.stem: A retail support agent built on the Messages API sends 30 tool definitions and a 12,000-token policy system prompt on every turn, with a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. Chats often run past 50 turns, and the agent began forgetting facts the customer stated early: the order number, the refund amount already approved, the delivery deadline. To fix that, an engineer inserted a "Case facts" block at the top of the system prompt, regenerated every turn from the conversation, together with the current timestamp. Fact recall improved, but usage now shows cache_read_input_tokens near zero on every request, and both cost and time to first token rose. What is the best fix?

options.text: Keep the tools and policy system prompt byte-identical with the breakpoint at their end, and send the regenerated case-facts block and timestamp after that prefix, such as in the newest user turn.
options.rationale: Correct. Cache hits need a 100% identical prefix in tools, system, messages order; putting the per-turn content after the breakpoint lets the static prefix be read from cache while the case facts are still pinned into every request.

options.text: Switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so cache entries survive between turns of long chats, where customers often pause for longer than the default five minutes before replying.
options.rationale: TTL only helps when a later request has an identical prefix. The regenerated block at the top of the system prompt changes the prefix every turn, so entries never match no matter how long they live, and 1-hour writes cost more.

options.text: Remove the case-facts block and the timestamp and rely on the conversation history, since caching makes resending the full history cheap on every turn.
options.rationale: This restores cache hits but brings back the original failure: facts buried deep in a long history are recalled less reliably as context grows (context rot).

options.text: Add a second cache_control breakpoint directly on the case-facts block, keeping the first one at the end of the policy text, so the facts and the policy are each cached and read back separately.
options.rationale: A breakpoint on a block that changes every turn writes a fresh cache entry (billed at the higher cache write rate) on every request and never produces a read; and because the block sits at the top of the system prompt, it still invalidates everything after it.

questions.explanation: Order the prompt from most stable to least stable: tools, static system instructions, then per-turn content, with the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix. Pin critical case facts into every request rather than trusting long history, but place them after the cached prefix so they do not invalidate it.
questions.verification_note: Length rebalance (2026-10-05): distractors b, c and d lengthened with still-wrong detail their existing rationales already refute (the 5-minute default TTL matches d5-004); key tightened with the byte-identical static prefix, breakpoint placement, and per-turn content after the prefix kept.

questions.stem: Every night a finance team extracts line items from about 30,000 scanned invoices into a fixed JSON schema. Downstream reports only need the results within 24 hours, and the team has been asked to cut the job's API cost. The current script fires synchronous Messages API calls from 200 parallel workers. Runs are noisy: many requests fail with 429 errors, and about 3% of saved outputs end partway through an object and fail JSON parsing, even though those responses returned HTTP 200. Which changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Retry every failed request, including 400 invalid_request_error responses, with exponential backoff until it succeeds.
options.rationale: A 400 means a problem with the request's format or content, so resending it unchanged fails the same way. Backoff retries are for transient errors such as 429, 500, and 529.

options.text: Submit the nightly run through the Message Batches API, giving each invoice a custom_id and matching results by that ID.
options.rationale: Correct. The work is bulk and not latency sensitive: batch usage is billed at 50% of standard prices, most batches finish within an hour, and results are available within 24 hours. Results can return in any order, so custom_id is how you match them.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 so the model stops ending responses partway through an object.
options.rationale: The cut-off outputs come from hitting the max_tokens output limit, which the API reports as stop_reason max_tokens; sampling temperature does not change the output cap.

options.text: Raise the worker count to 500 so the run finishes before rate limits reset.
options.rationale: More concurrency pushes harder against the same rate limits; the docs advise ramping traffic gradually to avoid acceleration limits, and the job has no latency need that justifies it.

options.text: Check stop_reason on every response and re-run any with "max_tokens" using a higher max_tokens value, instead of trying to repair the partial JSON.
options.rationale: Correct. A truncated response still returns HTTP 200; stop_reason max_tokens means the output may be incomplete and not match the schema, and the documented fix is to retry with a higher max_tokens.

questions.explanation: Match the API to the latency need: bulk work with a deadline measured in hours belongs in the Message Batches API at half price, matched back by custom_id. Always branch on stop_reason, because truncation (max_tokens) and refusals arrive as HTTP 200 and silently corrupt structured output if unchecked.
questions.verification_note: No drift found: batch pricing (50 percent), the 24-hour window, custom_id matching, and the max_tokens retry guidance all match current docs. Kept volatile because the pricing and timing figures are product numbers that can change.

questions.stem: A request marks a prompt block with cache_control {"type": "ephemeral"} and sets no ttl. How long does the cache entry live, and what extends it?

options.text: 1 hour from the write, and it cannot be extended
options.rationale: The 1-hour lifetime is opt-in through ttl "1h" at a higher write cost; it is not the default.

options.text: 24 hours, matching the Message Batches API window
options.rationale: The 24-hour figure belongs to batch processing, not to prompt cache lifetime.

options.text: 5 minutes, and each later read pays the cache write price to extend it
options.rationale: Reads are billed at the discounted cache read rate, and the refresh itself carries no additional cost.

options.text: 5 minutes, refreshed at no extra cost each time the cached content is used
options.rationale: Correct. The default lifetime is 5 minutes, measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, and every hit refreshes it for free.

questions.explanation: The default ephemeral cache lives 5 minutes and each cache hit resets the clock at no extra cost. If gaps between requests (including long streaming responses) exceed that, opt into ttl "1h", which costs more to write.
questions.verification_note: No drift found: the 5-minute default with free refresh on each hit matches current docs. Kept volatile because TTL options and cache write multipliers are product numbers that can change.

questions.stem: Mid-session you told Claude Code to return Result types instead of throwing. After a compaction it throws again. What best keeps the rule in effect across future compactions, manual or automatic?

options.text: Restate the rule in chat, prefixed with IMPORTANT
options.rationale: The rule still lives only in the conversation, which is exactly what compaction summarizes away.

options.text: Add the rule to the project-root CLAUDE.md
options.rationale: Correct. Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: Claude Code re-reads it from disk and re-injects it after /compact.

options.text: Run /compact Focus on the Result-type rule each time you compact
options.rationale: Custom /compact instructions shape that one manual summary, but the rule still lives only in conversation, so a later automatic compaction can drop it again.

options.text: Use /clear instead of /compact when the context fills
options.rationale: /clear resets the context window entirely, so a conversation-only rule is lost even more completely.

questions.explanation: Anything given only in conversation is subject to summarization. Project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after compaction, so durable rules belong there; you can also add compaction guidance to CLAUDE.md itself.

questions.stem: A platform team pays for Claude Code with API keys. One engineer runs long refactoring sessions on Opus and, several times an hour, uses /model to drop to Haiku for mechanical edits such as renames and import fixes, then switches back to Opus for design questions. His per-session cost is far above teammates doing similar work. His statusline, which reads the API usage fields, shows cache_creation_input_tokens jumping to roughly the size of the whole conversation on the first request after each switch, and those turns are noticeably slow. He still wants the cheaper model to handle the mechanical edits. What is the best change?

options.text: Switch his sessions to the one-hour cache TTL, since the misses come from the cached conversation expiring while he spends a few minutes on the other model.
options.rationale: Each model has its own cache, and Claude Code's docs say a switch makes the next request read the whole history with no cache hits, so the cause is the switch, not expiry. A one-hour TTL also bills cache writes at a higher rate.

options.text: Create a custom slash command for the mechanical edits whose frontmatter sets model to haiku, so he no longer has to switch with /model by hand.
options.rationale: A skill or command that names a different model runs in the main conversation, so that turn is itself a model switch and reads the entire history with no cache hits. It automates the expensive switch instead of removing it.

options.text: Run /compact right before each switch so the model he switches to only has a short summary to reprocess instead of the full conversation history.
options.rationale: Compaction replaces the working history with a summary, losing detail several times an hour mid-task, and each one is an extra summarization request that invalidates the conversation cache. The switch still misses; the miss is just smaller.

options.text: Keep the main session on Opus and hand the mechanical edits to a subagent whose model is haiku, which keeps its own cache apart from the parent's prefix.
options.rationale: Correct. A subagent works in its own context with its own cache, and from the parent's side its call and result simply append to the conversation. Routing side tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku is a documented use of subagents.

questions.explanation: In Claude Code each model has its own prompt cache, so switching models mid-task (with /model, opusplan, or a command's model frontmatter) reprocesses the whole conversation uncached. Pick the session model up front and route cheap side work to a subagent, whose separate context leaves the main conversation's cached prefix untouched.
questions.verification_note: Claude Code prompt caching page: each model has its own cache; /model, opusplan and a skill or command whose frontmatter names another model are model switches that read the entire history with no cache hits; a subagent warms its own cache and leaves the parent's prefix intact; compaction invalidates the conversation layer. Sub-agents page lists routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku. Option a no longer names the promptCacheTtl setting (v2.1.242 or later), so the item rests on the per-model cache principle.

questions.stem: Your team runs an internal dependency-upgrade agent on the Messages API, using a model with a 1M-token context window. One session works through a monorepo for hours, calling a run_tests tool whose results are 15,000 to 30,000 tokens of logs, plus read_file and edit_file. To control growth, an engineer enabled tool result clearing (clear_tool_uses_20250919) with a 40,000-token trigger and the default keep of 3. Two problems followed. Past the trigger, context_management.applied_edits shows a clearing on almost every request, and cache_creation_input_tokens stays high while cache reads fall. Late in a run, the agent no longer knows which tests failed earlier and re-runs suites it already analyzed. Which change best fixes both problems?

options.text: Turn context editing off and rely on the 1M-token window, so the history stays byte-identical for caching and every earlier test log remains readable.
options.rationale: Caching would recover, but hours of large logs push recall down as the context grows (context rot) and can still outrun the window; cached tokens still occupy the context window.

options.text: Set clear_at_least so each clearing frees a large block at once, and add the memory tool so the agent records failing tests before results are cleared.
options.rationale: Correct. clear_at_least skips clearing unless enough tokens can be freed to justify breaking the cache, so rewrites happen far less often. With the memory tool present, Claude gets an automatic warning near the clearing threshold and can save findings to memory files first.

options.text: Lower the trigger to 20,000 tokens and set keep to 1, so less old log text sits in context and every request sends a smaller prefix to the API.
options.rationale: Clearing earlier and keeping fewer results makes clearing more frequent, which invalidates the cache even more often, and removes findings sooner with nothing preserving them.

options.text: Move the cache breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the entries written before each clearing stay alive long enough for later requests in the run to read them.
options.rationale: Clearing replaces content inside the prefix, so an old entry stops matching after the cleared point no matter how long it lives. 1-hour writes also cost 2x base input instead of 1.25x.

questions.explanation: Tool result clearing invalidates the cached prefix wherever it removes content, so batch it with clear_at_least to make each cache rewrite worthwhile. Clearing also throws findings away, so pair it with the memory tool (or exclude_tools for results that must stay) to save what matters outside the context window before it is cleared.
questions.verification_note: Drift: context editing is still a beta (header context-management-2025-06-27) and current docs now name server-side compaction as the primary strategy for long-running agents, with context editing for more specialized needs. Volatile because strategy type names, defaults (trigger 100,000 input tokens, keep 3 tool uses) and cache write multipliers can change.

questions.stem: A legal-tech team's clause-extraction service sends each contract bundle, often 600,000 to 900,000 tokens, in a single Messages API request with max_tokens set to 32,000. Bundle sizes were budgeted with token counts measured months ago on Claude Opus 4.6. The team just moved the service to Claude Opus 4.7, which also has a 1M-token context window. Since the move, some requests fail with a 400 "prompt is too long" error, and others return HTTP 200 with extraction JSON that stops partway through, although the same bundles worked before the move. Which changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Re-count each bundle with the token counting endpoint using the Opus 4.7 model ID, and split any bundle whose count plus max_tokens would not fit.
options.rationale: Correct. Opus 4.7 introduced a newer tokenizer that produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, and the endpoint counts under the tokenizer of the model you pass, so counts measured on the older model no longer hold.

options.text: Add the 1M-context beta header to every request, since without it the API falls back to a 200k-token window for very long contract inputs like these.
options.rationale: For every model with a 1M-token window, 1M is the default and no beta header is needed; a smaller window is not what is rejecting these requests.

options.text: Mark the end of each bundle with a cache_control breakpoint so the cached contract tokens stop counting against the model's 1M-token context window.
options.rationale: Cached prefixes still occupy the context window; prompt caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.

options.text: Check stop_reason on every response and treat model_context_window_exceeded as a truncated result to re-run on a smaller split.
options.rationale: Correct. On Claude 4.5 and newer models the API accepts a request whose input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, and if generation reaches the limit it stops with model_context_window_exceeded; the docs say to treat that response as truncated.

options.text: Raise max_tokens to 128,000, the output cap for these models, so the model has enough room to finish the extraction JSON for even the largest bundles.
options.rationale: Input and output share one context window, so a higher max_tokens adds no room: generation still stops at the window limit, and inputs over 1M tokens still get a 400.

questions.explanation: Token budgets are tied to a model's tokenizer, so re-count with the token counting endpoint (free, with its own rate limit) using the model you are moving to. Near the limit, an input that alone exceeds the window gets a 400, while one that fits but leaves too little room ends with stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded and must be treated as truncated.
questions.verification_note: Drift: the newer tokenizer (about 30 percent more tokens) arrived with Claude Opus 4.7, likely after exam-era material was written, and exam-era material may still say a 1M-token window needs a beta header, which current docs say is not needed for any model with a 1M window. Volatile because tokenizer ratios, context window sizes and the 128k output cap can change. The context-windows page says the overflow behavior applies to Claude 4.5 models and newer; the stop-reasons page says Sonnet 4.5 and newer; both cover Opus 4.7.

questions.stem: Each turn your app appends about 30 new text blocks and puts cache_control only on the last block. Earlier content never changes, yet cache_read_input_tokens stays at 0. What fixes it?

options.text: Switch the breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so the previous turn's entry has not yet expired
options.rationale: Expiry is not the cause: the previous entry sits 30 blocks back, outside the 20-block lookback window, so no lifetime makes it reachable.

options.text: Move cache_control to the first block so everything after it is cached as well
options.rationale: A breakpoint caches the prefix up to and including its own block, so this caches only the first block and leaves the conversation uncached.

options.text: Also keep a breakpoint where the previous turn ended, since lookback checks 20 blocks
options.rationale: Correct. Lookback walks back at most 20 positions from each breakpoint and only finds entries earlier requests wrote; a second breakpoint at the previous turn's end starts a window that finds that write.

options.text: Put cache_control on each of the 30 new blocks so every block is cached on its own
options.rationale: A request can define at most 4 cache breakpoints, and caching works by prefix, not block by block.

questions.explanation: Cache reads look backward from each breakpoint for entries that earlier requests wrote, but only 20 blocks deep. When a turn adds more blocks than that, add a second breakpoint near the previous write (a request can use up to 4).
questions.verification_note: The stem says text blocks on purpose: on the Claude API a run of consecutive tool_use blocks, or of consecutive tool_result blocks, counts as one lookback position. Volatile because the 20-block lookback and the 4-breakpoint limit are product numbers that can change.

questions.stem: Server-side compaction returned a compaction block, and your app keeps the conversation history itself. What must later requests do so Claude keeps the summarized context?

options.text: Send that compaction block back in messages on every later request, content unchanged
options.rationale: Correct. The API keeps no conversation state: the block stands in for the summarized messages only when you send it, and a request that leaves it out gives Claude no summary.

options.text: Nothing extra, since the API stores the summary server-side and applies it automatically
options.rationale: The summary lives only in the block returned to you, and the docs require passing it back on subsequent requests.

options.text: Move the summary text into the system prompt and drop the compaction block from messages
options.rationale: The API expects the compaction block itself in messages, and rewriting the system prompt at each compaction also invalidates the system and messages caches.

options.text: Send the block once on the next request; after that its content is held in the prompt cache
options.rationale: Caching only speeds up a prefix you resend; it never supplies content you leave out, so dropping the block later drops the summary.

questions.explanation: Compaction is not server-side state. With threshold compaction the API ignores the blocks before the compaction block, and with on-demand compaction you replace the summarized messages with it, but either way the client keeps sending the block, exactly as returned, on every later request.
questions.verification_note: Drift: current docs offer two server-side variants, threshold compaction (compact_20260112 under beta compact-2026-01-12) and on-demand compaction (beta compact-2026-09-04, newer than exam-era material). They place the block differently (after the summarized messages versus first in messages) but both require sending it back on every later request. Volatile because both are betas.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions job runs `claude -p` after each failed nightly test run. Claude reads the test reports, calls create_issue on the team's MCP server once for each newly failing test, then posts a summary comment on the release PR. Because the step sometimes ended with "API Error: Repeated 529 Overloaded errors", an engineer wrapped it in a retry action that reruns the whole command, up to three times, whenever it exits non-zero. During last week's capacity incident, the first attempt filed six issues and then failed; the second attempt filed the same six issues again and posted a second PR comment. The team wants the job to ride out capacity errors without repeating work it already did. What should they change?

options.text: Keep the rerun wrapper but add exponential backoff with jitter between attempts (about 2, 4, then 8 minutes), so each rerun starts only after the capacity incident has had time to clear.
options.rationale: Spacing the reruns lowers the odds of hitting the same overload, but each rerun is a fresh session that starts the work over, so the issues and the PR comment already created are created again.

options.text: Add idempotentHint: true to the create_issue tool's MCP annotations, so Claude Code treats repeated calls as safe and skips any issue it already filed during an earlier attempt.
options.rationale: Annotations are optional hints that describe a tool's behavior, and clients must treat them as untrusted unless the server is trusted; they do not deduplicate calls across sessions, and a tool that files a new issue on every call is not idempotent, so the hint would misdescribe it.

options.text: Drop the whole-command rerun, let Claude Code's own request retries ride out the 529s (raising their limit for unattended runs), and make create_issue return a test's open issue.
options.rationale: Correct. Claude Code retries capacity errors per request and does not re-run a request once a tool call has completed, because that could execute the call twice; for unattended runs, CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 keeps retrying 429 and 529 errors instead of failing after CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES; and an idempotent create_issue (look up by test ID first) makes any rerun that still happens harmless.

options.text: Move the job onto the Message Batches API, which absorbs capacity errors within its 24-hour processing window and returns an errored result for the run instead of failing the step.
options.rationale: Batches run individual Messages API requests asynchronously, not a Claude Code session with its MCP tool loop, and errored results still have to be resubmitted by you, so nothing here prevents duplicate issues.

questions.explanation: Retry at the narrowest safe level: Claude Code's own request-level retries avoid re-running a request after a tool call has completed, while rerunning the whole agent repeats every side effect. Because some reruns are unavoidable, also make side-effecting tools idempotent, for example by keying creates on a stable ID and returning the existing record.
questions.verification_note: Drift: CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG (v2.1.186 and later; on v2.1.199 and later it also raises the retry count for other transient errors) and the rule that Claude Code does not re-run a request after a tool call has completed come from current Claude Code error docs. The key was reworded so it names no flag and rests on the durable principle: retry at the request level and make side-effecting tools idempotent. idempotentHint is defined in the Agent SDK TypeScript reference; the MCP tools spec says clients must treat annotations as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.

questions.stem: A claims team uses Claude with structured outputs to extract 14 fields, such as policy number, loss date, claimant name and reserve amount, from adjuster reports. Prompt changes ship after an engineer eyeballs ten outputs. Last month a tweak that fixed date formatting quietly broke policy-number extraction on handwritten reports, and nobody noticed for two weeks because every output still validated against the schema. The team now also wants to try a cheaper model. They have three years of past reports whose fields were keyed in by hand and checked by auditors. What should they put in place before the next prompt or model change?

options.text: A CI check that runs each candidate prompt on a few hundred recent reports and blocks the change if any output fails to parse or does not validate against the JSON schema.
options.rationale: Every output already validated against the schema during last month's regression, so this check would have passed; it tests the shape of the output, not whether the policy numbers are right.

options.text: An LLM grader that uses the same model as the extractor to score each output from 1 to 10 for overall quality, blocking any change that lowers the average score.
options.rationale: When golden values exist, code-based grading is faster and more reliable; a vague overall-quality score hides which field broke, and the docs advise detailed rubrics and a different model from the one that produced the output.

options.text: A review panel in which two senior adjusters hand-grade the 50 hardest reports from the past year, checking every field, before each prompt or model release.
options.rationale: Human grading is slow and expensive and best avoided where automation works; 50 hand-picked hard cases also do not mirror the real distribution, and the docs favor more automatically graded cases over fewer hand-graded ones.

options.text: A few hundred audited reports sampled to match production, handwritten ones included, with code comparing each extracted field to its keyed value, run on every change.
options.rationale: Correct. It mirrors the real task distribution including the edge case that regressed, grades by code against known-good values (fast, objective, reproducible), and shows results per field, so each prompt or model change is checked before it ships.

questions.explanation: Schema validity is not correctness. When you have verified answers, build a regression suite from representative cases, including the edge cases that broke before, grade each field by code against the golden values, and run it on every prompt and model change so a fix in one field cannot silently break another.

questions.stem: Your platform team runs an internal pull-request review bot on the Messages API. A CI webhook sends one request per push, and after a release branch merges, several hundred PRs rebase within a minute. Last week the team opened the bot to all 12 engineering teams at once, and daily traffic jumped about tenfold overnight. Since then, reviews fail in bursts with 429 rate_limit_error, although the Console Usage page shows the organization peaking well under its tier's ITPM and OTPM limits. Each worker runs its own retry loop that resends a failed request every second and ignores the retry-after header, so the workers retry in lockstep. One afternoon some requests also failed with 529 overloaded_error, and an engineer wants to request a higher usage tier because of them. Which changes should the team make? Select TWO.

options.text: Lower max_tokens on every review request from 8,192 to 2,048 so that each request reserves less of the output-tokens-per-minute budget while it is running.
options.rationale: OTPM is evaluated as output tokens are produced and counts only the tokens actually generated; max_tokens does not factor into OTPM, so lowering it frees no budget and can cut reviews short.

options.text: Swap the lockstep loops for the SDK's retries, which back off exponentially and honor retry-after, and pace new requests from the rate limit headers.
options.rationale: Correct. retry-after gives the seconds to wait and earlier retries fail, so lockstep one-second retries only add load. The SDK retries rate limits and 5xx errors with exponential backoff, honoring retry-after, and the anthropic-ratelimit-*-remaining headers show headroom for pacing bursts, which can trip limits enforced over intervals shorter than a minute.

options.text: Scale the rollout back and re-expand it a few teams at a time so usage grows gradually, since a sharp jump in usage can trigger 429s from acceleration limits.
options.rationale: Correct. The rate limits docs warn that a sharp increase in an organization's usage can produce 429 errors from acceleration limits, and advise ramping up traffic gradually and keeping usage patterns consistent.

options.text: Request a higher usage tier in the Console, since the 529 overloaded errors show that the organization went over its own rate limits during the afternoon spike.
options.rationale: A 529 overloaded_error means the API is under high traffic across all users, not that the organization hit its limits, which return 429 rate_limit_error. Usage is already under the tier limits, so a higher tier fixes neither error.

options.text: Hold every failed request until the start of the next clock minute, when the per-minute limits reset, so the retried requests all find a full budget waiting.
options.rationale: The API uses a token bucket that replenishes capacity continuously rather than resetting at fixed intervals, and releasing all retries at the minute boundary recreates the burst.

questions.explanation: A 429 is your organization's own limit and tells you when to come back: honor retry-after, back off instead of retrying in lockstep, smooth bursts because limits can be enforced over intervals shorter than a minute, and grow traffic gradually to avoid acceleration limits. A 529 means the API itself is overloaded across all users, so retry it with backoff rather than changing tiers.
questions.verification_note: Rewritten in the verify pass: the earlier draft (refusal stop_reason, fallback model, refusal metrics) duplicated d4-008. New topic is rate limits and traffic shaping, written from the rate limits and errors pages: retry-after semantics, rate limit response headers, token bucket replenishment, enforcement over shorter intervals, acceleration limits, OTPM ignoring max_tokens, 529 as API-wide overload, and SDK retries with exponential backoff that honor retry-after. The docs do not mention jitter, so no option relies on it.

questions.stem: A Message Batch reaches its 24-hour limit while 3,000 of its requests have not yet been sent to the model. What happens to those 3,000 requests?

options.text: They keep processing past the limit, and their results show up once done, within the 29-day results window
options.rationale: Batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours; the 29 days is how long results stay downloadable after creation, not extra processing time.

options.text: Each gets an expired result and is not billed; results for requests that already finished stay available
options.rationale: Correct. Requests the batch could not send to the model before its 24-hour expiration get the expired result type and are not billed, and results become accessible after 24 hours even if not every request completed.

options.text: The whole batch is canceled and every result is discarded, including requests that had already succeeded
options.rationale: Expiry does not throw away finished work: results are available when all messages complete or after 24 hours, whichever comes first. canceled is a separate result type for a batch the user canceled.

options.text: Each gets an errored result of type api_error and is billed for the input tokens already processed
options.rationale: errored covers invalid requests and internal server errors, and errored, canceled and expired results are all unbilled.

questions.explanation: A batch ends at 24 hours at the latest: finished requests keep their results (downloadable for 29 days from creation), and requests never sent to the model come back as expired at no charge. Match expired results by custom_id and send those requests again in a new batch if you still need them.
questions.verification_note: No drift found: the 24-hour expiration, unbilled expired results, and 29-day result availability match current docs. Kept volatile because these are product limits that can change.

questions.stem: A Messages API request that embeds 45 MB of base64-encoded PDF scans fails with 413 request_too_large. What should the client do?

options.text: Shrink the request instead of retrying: upload the PDFs with the Files API and send file_id references, or split them up
options.rationale: Correct. 413 means the body exceeds the 32 MB Messages API limit, so resending the same bytes fails every time; the PDF docs suggest the Files API with file_id references to keep payloads small, and splitting documents when large PDFs still fail.

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, since the SDK treats 413 as a transient error that clears once API load drops
options.rationale: 413 is a size limit, not a transient fault; the SDK's automatic retries cover connection errors, rate limits and 5xx errors, and on the direct API Cloudflare rejects the oversized body before it reaches the API servers.

options.text: Set stream: true, since streaming sends the request body in chunks and is exempt from the 32 MB Messages request limit
options.rationale: Streaming changes how the response is delivered, as incremental server-sent events; the request body still has to fit within the 32 MB Messages API limit.

options.text: Lower max_tokens until the input plus the largest possible output fits within the 32 MB limit for one Messages request
options.rationale: max_tokens caps how many tokens Claude generates; it does not shrink the request body, which is what the 32 MB request size limit measures.

questions.explanation: Classify errors before retrying: 413 is about the request's size, so retries, streaming and max_tokens changes cannot help. Keep payloads small by referencing uploaded files by file_id, or split the work into smaller requests.
questions.verification_note: No drift found: the 32 MB Messages API request limit, the 413 request_too_large type, and the Files API file_id guidance for large PDFs match current docs. Kept volatile because request size limits are product numbers that vary by platform and can change.
